title: Annotations on the Definitive Guide to the Western Land
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: This book (The Definitive Guide to the Western Land) is a record of the instructions of the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing. Having come from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whatever he spoke was the essential mystery of practice. If one can contemplate it constantly and strive to follow it, one will surely be reborn in the highest grade.

This book
(The Definitive Guide to the Western Land)

is a record of the instructions of the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing. Having come from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whatever he spoke was the essential mystery of practice. If one can contemplate it from time to time and strive to follow it, one will surely be reborn in the highest grade.
[Definitive Guide to the West] This is an exact indication: to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is the genuine path of practice.

blocks.text: Preface to The Definitive Guide to the Western Land

inline.s: [In the summer of the year Ding-wei, I called at the abbot's quarters of Master Xueshan. He brought out a book and gave it to me, saying: 'This is a precious raft, and its origins are most extraordinary.']
In the summer of the year Ding-wei (
), I (the author of this preface) called at the abbot's quarters of Master Xueshan. He brought out a book and handed it to me, saying
This is a precious boat for crossing the bitter sea of birth and death! And its origins are most extraordinary."
[At the end of the Ming dynasty, eight friends of Wucheng practiced together the way of the mystics, daily inviting the planchette immortals to discuss their arts. When it came to the last
zú
at the end)
a spirit came, and what it spoke differed from all the other immortals. So they served it every day and grew most familiar
xiá
intimate)

with it. After a long while, it suddenly urged them to recite the Buddha's name. They asked: 'Can reciting the Buddha's name lead to the Way?' It replied: 'It is the very method.' They all recited: 'Namo Buddha.' It said: 'It is not to be recited that way.' They asked how it should be done. It said: 'You must join your palms and, with utmost sincerity, bow toward the West and recite: "Namo Amitābha Buddha."' They followed it. It then explained to them in fine detail the practice of Buddha-recitation, bidding them to cast off the false and return to the true, and to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. It then began to reveal its past causes, the Bodhisattva's name, and manifested rare fragrances and heavenly flowers and every kind of auspicious sign. And these eight, all of them, turned from their wrong practices and returned to right faith.]

Toward the end of the Ming dynasty, eight friends of Wucheng (present-day Wu County of Jiangsu Province, under Suzhou City) practiced together the way of the mystics, daily setting up the planchette and inviting the immortals, discoursing on the arts of immortal cultivation. At last, a spirit descended with a message, and what it spoke was very different from the other immortals. So they waited on it daily and sought its instruction, growing ever more familiar and convinced. After a long while, the spirit suddenly urged them to recite the Buddha's name. They asked: 'Can reciting the Buddha's name bring one to the Way?' It answered: 'It is the wondrous method for attaining the Way.' They all recited together: 'Namo Buddha.' The spirit said: 'It is not to be recited that way.' They asked: 'How, then, is it to be recited?' It said: 'You must join your palms and, with your most sincere heart, bow toward the West, and recite: "Namo Amitābha Buddha."' They followed its instruction and bowed to Amitābha Buddha. Thereupon the spirit gave them a detailed and subtle exposition of the practice of Buddha-recitation, bidding them to cast off the false and return to the true, and to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. It also began to reveal the causes of a past life (eight hundred years earlier the Bodhisattva had been their teacher), its own Bodhisattva title (the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing), and manifested rare fragrances and heavenly flowers, and all manner of auspicious signs. And these eight all renounced their wrong practices and returned to right faith.
[Planchette (
jī

)] A method of divination, also called 'the phoenix basket,' 'the lowered brush,' 'inviting the immortals,' and other names. In planchette divination, one person plays the role of one possessed by a deity; such a person is called a luan-sheng. The deity then possesses the luan-sheng and writes characters to convey its instruction (an oracle). Through this means the faithful communicate with the deity. [Phoenix (luan)] The phoenix-luan is a mythical bird of ancient China, the messenger of Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West, responsible for bringing tidings from the deities. Thus 'phoenix' also carries the meaning of conveying a divine message. [Utmost sincerity (zhi xin)] The most sincere heart.
[Wuxiu, the teacher of the eight, was the leader among them. The Bodhisattva bade him go to Master Sanmei to receive the vinaya
(receive the precepts)
and perfect the form of a monk. At first the master made it difficult for him; but when he saw the Bodhisattva's 'Moon Gatha,' he bowed toward the West and had him shaved. This was because
(this was because)

when the Bodhisattva first came, the gathering took him for an immortal and, taking the moon as the theme, asked for a verse. He then gave them this gatha: 'One moon's light holds a thousand worlds; countless bodies shine on the deluded. Know that the essence is originally one; motionless, majestic, it is the working of change.']

Wuxiu was the teacher among the eight. The Bodhisattva sent him to Master Sanmei to be shaved and receive the precepts, so as to perfect the form of a monk. At first Master Sanmei made it difficult for him (at first, seeing that Wuxiu had come with an oracle from the planchette altar, he thought the gods and spirits had sent him, and refused to shave his head or give him the precepts); later, when he saw the 'Moon Gatha' shown by the Bodhisattva, he knew this was the command of a great Bodhisattva come from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so bowed toward the West and had him shaved. This was because, when the Bodhisattva first came to the planchette altar, the gathering thought he was an immortal, and took the moon as the theme to request a verse. The Bodhisattva therefore spoke this gatha:
'A single moon
(the Bodhisattva's reward-body)
shines
(the Bodhisattva's emanation-body)
over
(encompassing)
a thousand worlds
(the three thousand great chiliocosms)
, countless bodies shine on the deluded
(sending forth countless emanation-bodies to save the countless deluded and upside-down beings)
, know that the essence is originally one
(should understand that the Bodhisattva's reward-body is always just this one)
, motionless, majestic, the working of change

(though with countless emanation-bodies it responds to occasion and saves countless beings throughout the three thousand great chiliocosms, its reward-body in the Land of Ultimate Bliss remains ever still and unmoving)
[Master Sanmei] That is the famous Lawyer Sanmei (for details see
A Dream of Wandering

). All his life he propagated the vinaya, knew in advance the time of his coming and going, and passed away at a set time while seated. On the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month of the first year of Hongguang of the Ming dynasty (

) Master Sanmei returned from Suzhou to Bao Hua Mountain in Nanjing, and the assembly bowed to him and asked after his health. The master smiled and said: 'Today I make an appointment with you (I tell you in advance now): between three days and seven days from now, will I not be free from the hanging? (I will be reborn freely; the original text means: can I not be reborn freely?)' Hearing this the assembly all wept in sorrow. The master said: 'Birth and death are but an illusion; in truth there is no coming and going. Why do you weep?' When the first day of the month came, the master looked over the almanac and said: 'At the si hour of the fourth day (in the morning from

o'clock) I will enter nirvāṇa!' Thereupon in the abbot's room he rang the wooden gong and gathered the assembly, transmitted the Dharma to Lawyer Jianyue (the author of A Dream of Wandering), entrusted him with the affairs of the monastery, and settled the matters of his own passing. When the fourth day came he gathered the assembly again, drew water and bathed. He then taught: 'When the water dries up I will go. Do not think in terms of coming or going; you must not wear mourning or weep, you must not send word of my passing far and wide — cast aside all worldly rites, every one of them. After three days bury me on Dragon Mountain of the monastery.' He then bade the assembly recite the Buddha's name; when the water had dried up he sat cross-legged, smiled, and passed away. The monastery only recited the scriptures with utmost sincerity for three days, and held no worldly ceremonies at all.
[Suspended release (xuan jie)]

To be freed from being hung upside down: delivered from a state of distress. [Three bodies] The Dharma-body, the reward-body, and the emanation-body. The Dharma-body is the ever-abiding, unperishing true nature that all beings inherently possess; only sentient beings are deluded and do not reveal it, while buddhas and bodhisattvas are awakened and realize it. The reward-body is the body accomplished through the wisdom and merit of a buddha or bodhisattva. The emanation-body is the body that a buddha or bodhisattva manifests in response to the capacities and circumstances of sentient beings.
[It began on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month of the year Gui-wei of Chongzhen of the Ming, and lasted until
qì
ended at)

the second day of the tenth month of the year Ding-hai of Shunzhi of the Qing — twenty-four assemblies in all. What was spoken was all the essential mystery of practice; and because the gatha contained the line 'definitively pointing out the correct path of practice,' the record was therefore named The Definitive Guide to the Western Land.]
The Bodhisattva's exposition of the practice of Buddha-recitation began on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month of the year Gui-wei of Chongzhen of the Ming (
) and ended on the second day of the tenth month of the year Ding-hai of Shunzhi of the Qing (

) — twenty-four assemblies in all. What was spoken was all the essential mystery of practice; and because the gatha the Bodhisattva spoke contained the line 'definitively pointing out the correct path of practice,' this record of instructions was therefore titled The Definitive Guide to the Western Land.
The above was spoken by Master Xueshan.
[When I read it, my body and mind leapt with joy, no less than
bù chì,
as though)

sweet ambrosia dripping into a parched heart! So I could not cease exclaiming at its wonder. Master Xueshan said: 'At first I too did not believe it; but after I had read it, my spirit shone forth, and even were I to try I could not disbelieve.' I said: 'In the past, in his causal ground, the Bodhisattva had a great affinity with these eight; because his compassionate remembrance was deep, he used skillful means to come to the planchette and guide them. How can this be compared with the company of those who respond through the planchette! Moreover, in his parting instructions the Bodhisattva said: "The planchette is established as a support for spirits and ghosts; it is not the constant work of a great Bodhisattva's transformational response." So how can this book be regarded as an ordinary planchette text?'

After reading it, I (the author of this preface) leapt with joy in body and mind, like sweet ambrosia dripping into a withered heart! So I could not stop exclaiming at its wonder. Master Xueshan said: 'At first I did not believe it either; but after I had finished reading it, my spirit shone forth, and even if I wanted to disbelieve I could not.' I said: 'In the past, in his causal ground, the Bodhisattva had a great affinity with these eight; because his compassionate remembrance was deep, he therefore used skillful means to come to the planchette and guide them. How can this be lumped together with the spirits and ghosts of the planchette! Moreover, in his parting instructions the Bodhisattva said: "The planchette is in itself a support for spirits and ghosts; it is not the constant work of a great Bodhisattva responding to occasion to save beings." So how can this book be looked upon as an ordinary planchette text?'

[At that time I at once wished to print it and circulate it, to benefit the many widely, but the causes were not yet joined. Up to now, in the spring of the year Ji-you, monks, laypeople, and fellow practitioners of the Way one and all leapt with joy and wished to contribute funds
(zī, the same as 'zi')

to help bring it to completion. There were even some who, reading it, wept, and weeping read on, abruptly giving up their beloved houses, clothes, and implements to go into the deep mountains and recite the Buddha's name. Is this not the great compassion without conditions, gathering and transforming sentient beings — a matter beyond thought? Thereupon I consulted with the two teachers Lingxi and Huiji, planning to have it printed. When the printing blocks
(zǐ, the carved blocks for printing)
were completed, I have related its whole course as such.]
At that time I at once wished to carve blocks and print the book for circulation, so as to benefit beings widely, but the causes were not yet complete. Up to now, in the spring of the year Ji-you (

), monks, laypeople, and fellow practitioners of the Way one and all leapt with joy and were willing to contribute funds to help print it. There were even some who, reading it, wept, and weeping read on, abruptly giving up their beloved houses, clothes, and implements to go into the deep mountains and recite the Buddha's name. Is this not the Bodhisattva's great compassion without conditions, gathering and transforming sentient beings — a matter beyond thought? Thereupon I consulted with the two teachers Lingxi and Huiji, and we planned to carve the blocks and print it. When the printing was finished, I have recorded the whole course of the matter as such.
[At that time, in the year Ji-you of Kangxi, on the sixteenth day of the ninth month
(the day after the full moon, that is, the sixteenth day of the lunar month)
, composed by Jin E, styled Langxi, a Pure-Land practitioner of ancient Wu.]
In the year Ji-you of Kangxi (
), on the sixteenth day of the ninth month, the Pure-Land practitioner of Wucheng, Jin E, styled Langxi, wrote this preface.

blocks.text: Postface to The Definitive Guide to the Western Land

inline.s: [The sages and holy men of antiquity are far removed from us today. Yet when we read their books and know their words, we may be certain they cannot have been forged; the judgment rests on principle alone. Since the Buddha's Dharma entered China, in these fifteen hundred years the heroic and clear-sighted ones who obtained a single scripture or a single verse, and with decisive faith entered and transcended birth and death, have been
(dài, nearly)
beyond counting. But shallow-witted people
(zhé, then)
peep at them with their own private opinions, saying they originate from Laozi and Zhuangzi
(Laozi and Zhuangzi)
and are forgeries made by their followers. Now the books of Laozi and Zhuangzi are here before us; take them and compare them with the Shurangama Sutra
the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra and the other scriptures
(to compare)
and the reason for their shallowness or depth, their agreement or divergence, is entirely
(wholly)
plain. If Laozi and Zhuangzi could not produce such works, can those who study Laozi and Zhuangzi produce them? This is the fault of those who cannot discern principle and indulge
(xùn, to follow crookedly)
their own private inclinations.]

The sages and holy men of antiquity are far removed from us now. Yet when we read their books and understand the principles they set forth, we may be certain that they cannot have been forged, because the judgment can be made on the basis of the principles spoken of in the books. Since the Buddha's Dharma came into China, in these fifteen hundred years the heroic and clear-sighted ones who obtained a single scripture or a single verse, and with decisive faith entered and transcended birth and death, are nearly beyond counting. But shallow-witted people peer at the Buddhist scriptures with their own private opinions, saying they originate from Laozi and Zhuangzi and are forgeries made by their disciples and their disciples' disciples. Now the books of Laozi and Zhuangzi are all here; compare them with the Shurangama Sutra, the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra and the other scriptures, and the shallowness or depth, the agreement or divergence, of the two is entirely clear. If Laozi and Zhuangzi could not write books such as the Shurangama Sutra and the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, could their disciples and their disciples' disciples write them? Those who say the Buddhist scriptures come from the hands of the disciples of Laozi and Zhuangzi are people who cannot discern the principles spoken of in the books, but follow their own private inclinations and talk recklessly!
[In recent ages the practice of the flying phoenix has prevailed; the sages and holy men of the three teachings
(Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism)

often respond according to the circumstances, spreading the Dharma and saving people — all out of an unwilling heart. When we read their books and know their words, we may be certain they cannot have been forged; here too the judgment rests on principle alone.]

In recent ages the work of the planchette has been practiced, and the sages of the three teachings (Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism) often respond according to circumstances, spreading the Dharma and saving people — all out of an unwilling heart (for because the planchette was then in vogue, the Bodhisattva had no choice but to come to the altar and deliver an oracle to save beings; this is walking in a non-path so as to reach the Buddha-path). Yet when we read the planchette texts they have written out, we know that the principles they speak of cannot have been forged, also because the principles spoken of in the planchette text can be used to judge whether it is the Bodhisattva's own speech or that of a spirit or ghost.
[At that time the planchette was in full vogue.]

The Ming dynasty honored Daoism, and the planchette came out of the Daoist school, so it was also highly regarded by those in high places, flourishing among the scholar-officials, and the middle and lower classes vied to imitate it; it flourished for a time, and continued without decline down to the Qing dynasty.

[The Definitive Guide to the Western Land is the Dharma spoken by the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing in the realm of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As a teaching it condemns wrong practices and points back to the Pure Land, expounds the wondrous truth of the one mind, and exhausts the mysterious gate of the upward path — truly a guide for those who study Buddhism.]

The book The Definitive Guide to the Western Land is the Dharma spoken by the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. His instructions condemn wrong practices and point back to the Pure Land, clarify the wondrous truth of the one mind, and exhaust the mysterious gate of the upward path — this truly is a guide for those who study Buddhism!
[The wondrous truth of the one mind.] "

One mind has the one-mindedness of practice (shi) and the one-mindedness of principle (li): without any other thought is the one-mindedness of practice (shi); entering into true reality is the one-mindedness of principle (li). 'Wondrous truth' means the subtle and exquisite true principle. 'Truth' means the reality that is not empty and not false.
[The mysterious gate of the upward path.] The utmost limit of the Chan (Zen) school is called 'the one road upward.' 'The mysterious gate of the upward path' is the doorway of that one road upward.
[I read it over and over, rose up
(arose)

and sighed: Alas! The land of the lotus flower is never apart from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is wholly within sentient beings. But these sentient beings do not know it in their daily use, and have never so much as aroused a single thought of dedication; so they go from delusion into delusion, drifting through long eons — is this not pitiful! The Bodhisattva's compassionate vow is deep and weighty; age after age he follows these beings, never abandoning them.]

I read it over and over, rose, and exclaimed: Alas! The land of the lotus is never apart from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is wholly within sentient beings. But these beings, using it daily, do not know it, and have never aroused so much as a single thought of dedication; so they go from delusion into delusion, drifting through long eons — is this not pitiful! The Bodhisattva's compassionate vow is deep and weighty; age after age he follows these beings and never abandons them in saving them.
[The land of the lotus is never apart from this very place; Amitābha Buddha is wholly within sentient beings.]
The Three-Periods Chant of Master Zhongfeng says:

Amitābha Buddha is my very mind, my own mind is Amitābha Buddha; the Pure Land is this very place, this very place is the Pure Land. Is it not that delusion and awakening differ on their own — how could there be a holy and a common, an other and a self?'

[How does the transformation of the flying phoenix differ from manifesting a body to teach the Dharma? One who reads this book and truly believes his own fundamental mind, practices as it teaches, and dedicates thought after thought, with no other distracting thought, until thought reaches its limit and emotion is emptied, freed and dwelling nowhere — though now dwelling in the five turbidities of the evil world, already his whole body sits within the lotus land. When the retribution of this body's conditions ends, in the snapping of a finger he is reborn there. This is fruit and this is cause, with no first and no last between them. But if one does not believe his own mind, and therefore does not believe in the Pure Land, and worse still suspects this book to be a forgery, then I can do nothing with him!]

How does the transformation of the planchette differ from manifesting a body to teach the Dharma? One who reads The Definitive Guide to the Western Land and truly believes his own fundamental mind, practices as it teaches, and dedicates thought after thought, with no distracting thought, until thought reaches its limit and emotion is emptied, freed and dwelling nowhere — though now dwelling in the five turbidities of the evil world, already his whole body sits within the lotus land. When the conditions of this body's retribution come to an end, in the snapping of a finger he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is fruit and this is cause, with no first and no last between them. But if one does not believe his own mind, and therefore does not believe in the Pure Land, and even suspects this book to be a forgery, then I have no way with him!
[Five turbidities.]

First, the turbidity of the age: the age meets with evil fortune and disasters arise again and again. Second, the turbidity of afflictions: people's hearts are filled with the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion. Third, the turbidity of beings: beings' faculties are lowly, with much suffering and little joy. Fourth, the turbidity of views: wrong views prevail and thought is confused. Fifth, the turbidity of life: sentient beings, retributed by evil karma, are worn in body and mind, and their lives are short.
[Retribution-conditions (bao yuan).]
The causes and conditions of retribution. Here it refers to the lifespan of this one lifetime.
[To have no recourse (mo ru zhi he).] To have no way
out, utterly helpless.
[This book I obtained from my friend Wang Guansan; there had been printing blocks, but recently
(not long ago)
they were destroyed by fire. My fellow villagers

(the worthies) will have it carved anew to circulate in the world. I have respectfully corrected its chapters and sentences, and set them in order. When it was done, I have written this preface as such.]

This book (The Definitive Guide to the Western Land) I obtained from my friend Wang Guansan; there had been printing blocks, but not long ago they were destroyed in a fire. My fellow villagers, the worthies, will have it carved anew and printed, so that it may circulate in the world. I respectfully corrected its chapters and sentences, and set them in order. The book being done, I have related the matter thus.
[My fellows (wu dang)] Our home village. Here the word 'dang' (fellows)
refers to the home village. 'Dang' is an ancient local household organization unit; five hundred families made up one dang.
[In the autumn, the eighth month, of the thirty-eighth year of Qianlong, composed by the later student of Donglin, Peng Shaosheng.]
In the eighth month of autumn of the thirty-eighth year of Qianlong (
), written as a preface by the later student of Donglin, Peng Shaosheng.

[Later student of Donglin.] 'Donglin' is Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu, the place where Master Huiyuan, the first patriarch of the Pure Land school, first established the Lotus Society. 'Later student' means a junior learner. [Peng Shaosheng (

)] A great lay practitioner and scholar of the Qing dynasty, a native of Changzhou (Wu County) of Jiangsu. His courtesy name was Yunchu, his style name Chimu, and he was also known as the Layman Erlin; his Buddhist name was Jiqing. Born into a family of scholar-officials, both his grandfather and his father were top-ranked jinshi, and his father rose to be Vice-Minister of War. Shaosheng was clever from childhood; at sixteen he became a xiucai, in the following year he passed the provincial examination as a juren, and in the next year he passed the palace examination as a jinshi, but he declined office. He once studied the books of the earlier Confucians, mastered the Neo-Confucianism of the Song and Ming, and was skilled in classical prose. Later he practiced the arts of Daoist cultivation, and after three years without success, because he read Buddhist books, he turned to Buddhism at twenty-nine, calling himself Guizhi (the Returner). Day by day he made ritual recitation his task, read the Great Canon, received the bodhisattva precepts, and practiced a pure vegetarian life. He further received the Pure Land teaching from Master Wenzue Dinggong, and went into seclusion at Wenxing Pavilion in Suzhou, diligently practicing the one-practice samadhi. Throughout his life he delighted in charity, devoted himself to spreading the Pure Land teaching, and wrote voluminously. His Treatise on the Resolution of Doubts of the One Vehicle argued for the unity of Buddhism and Confucianism; his Treatise on the Avatamsaka Buddha-Recitation Samadhi advocated the fusion of Chan and Pure Land; and his New Expositions on the Three Pure Land Sutras developed the meaning of the Pure Land doctrine. In addition he wrote Histories of Lay Practitioners, Biographies of Good Women, Records of the Sages of the Pure Land, and other works. That the Pure Land school flourished in recent times and surpassed all the others is largely due to his pioneering effort. He passed away in the first month of the first year of Jiaqing, at the age of fifty-seven.

inline.s: [At one time, the Bodhisattva came from the Land of Ultimate Bliss and descended upon the Saha
(the Saha world)
land of Cīna (China)
(in ancient times India called China 'Cīna')
of old
(in ancient times)
Gouwu
(Gouwu, present-day Wu County of Jiangsu, under Suzhou City)
. The disciples in the assembly, through
(because of)
past causes from a former life, received his transforming guidance. The Bodhisattva was about to reveal the Pure Land practice, and spoke this gatha:]

At one time, the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing came from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and descended upon Wu County of Jiangsu in China, within the Saha world. The disciples in the assembly, through past causes from a former life (eight hundred years earlier the Bodhisattva had been the teacher of the eight in the assembly), received his transforming guidance. The Bodhisattva was about to reveal the Pure Land practice, and spoke this gatha:
The essential Dharma of all buddhas is subtle, hidden, and beyond thought; because it is beyond thought, no one can fully proclaim it. Muni
(Śākyamuni Buddha)

, the great compassionate father, who pities sentient beings, spoke what cannot be spoken, guiding them for this life and the next. He further, by a special means, revealed the land of peace and bliss, causing beings to vow to be reborn there, cutting directly across all evil destinies. By
yóu
, an old form of 'from')

the Buddha Amitābha, whose great vows gather all kinds of beings: those who hear his name and are able to uphold it will surely be reborn, without doubt. If there is a person of great strength, single-mindedly mindful with an ever-constant heart, accomplishing the deep samadhi, he sees the Buddha before him. Now I, following the Buddha's teaching, will open the gate of guidance; mindful that you are all fallen into confusion, I precisely point out the correct path of practice. This is no small karmic bond; you should cherish it as a rare and hard-to-meet chance; the Western Land is vast beyond measure, and a single thought of faith is enough to reach it.]
The essential Dharma of all buddhas is subtle, hidden, and beyond thought; because it is beyond thought, no one can fully proclaim it.
Muni
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
, the great compassionate father, who pities sentient beings, spoke what cannot be spoken, guiding them for this life and the next.
He further, by a special means, revealed the land of peace and bliss
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, causing beings to vow to be reborn there, cutting straight across all evil destinies.
By
(from)
the Buddha Amitābha, whose great vows gather all kinds of beings: those who hear his name and are able to uphold it will surely be reborn, without doubt.
If there is a person of great strength, single-mindedly mindful with an ever-constant heart, accomplishing the deep samadhi
(accomplishing the profound Buddha-recitation samadhi)
, then before him too the Buddha appears.
Now I, following the Buddha's teaching, will open the gate of guidance; mindful that you are all fallen into confusion, I precisely point out the correct path of practice.
This is no small karmic bond; you should cherish it as a rare and hard-to-meet chance. The Western Land is vast beyond measure; a single thought of faith is enough to reach it.

[Land of peace and bliss (an-le sha)] The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Great vows gather all kinds of beings] With the forty-eight great vows he widely gathers beings of all capacities. [Precisely points out the correct path of practice]

He precisely points out the correct path of practice — the Pure Land practice. [Single-mindedly mindful with an ever-constant heart] Single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name, so that in the heart there is always only this one thought of the Buddha's name. This is supremely excellent; for details see
Single-Minded Buddha-Recitation
in the passage 'Single-minded Buddha-recitation is supremely excellent.'

[When the Bodhisattva had spoken the gatha, he bade the disciples read it aloud once. Again he said: 'You have all along studied and honored the mystic arts, your hearts sunk in wrong practices. Because my past affinity with you is deep and my compassionate remembrance great, I have come here to guide you. Now I have first set forth the Western Pure Land as the one path of right direction and right practice; but still fearing you cannot fully believe, I shall next tell you my name and what I have realized, that you may know the one who speaks this Dharma is a great Bodhisattva.]

When the Bodhisattva had spoken the gatha, he bade the disciples read it aloud once. Then he said: 'You have all along honored and studied the mystic arts, your hearts single-mindedly sunk in wrong practices. Because in the past I had a very deep affinity with you, and in compassion I think of you, I have come here to guide you. Now I have first set up the Pure Land practice as the path of right direction and right practice; but still fearing you cannot fully believe, I shall next tell you my name and what I have realized, that you may know that the one who speaks this Dharma is a great Bodhisattva.'

[Good man, in the past, in my causal ground, with the wondrously clear enlightened mind I illuminated all the lands everywhere, a mind that all sentient beings likewise possess. Thereupon, with that awakened, wondrous, supremely-awakened, clear and wondrous mind, I aroused countless wondrous practices and saved sentient beings. Therefore Amitābha Buddha confirmed my name, calling me 'Awakened, Bright, Wonderfully Acting' (Jue Ming Miao Xing). From this time forth you may take refuge, with no further doubt.' At that time the eight in the assembly all joined their palms and, with utmost sincerity, recited 'Namo to the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing,' bowed in reverence, and rose. The Bodhisattva said: 'Excellent. It is so.']

Good man, in the past, in my causal ground, with the wondrously clear enlightened mind (the originally-enlightened mind), I illuminated all the lands of the ten directions. This wondrously clear enlightened mind all sentient beings likewise possess, only they are deluded and do not reveal it. I then, with that awakened, wondrous, supremely-awakened, clear and wondrous mind, aroused countless wondrous practices and saved sentient beings. Therefore Amitābha Buddha confirmed me as Awakened, Bright, Wonderfully Acting (Jue Ming Miao Xing), and bestowed upon me the name 'Jue Ming Miao Xing.' From this time forth you may take refuge, and have no further doubt at all.' At that time the eight of the assembly all joined their palms, and with utmost sincerity recited 'Namo to the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing,' bowed in reverence, and rose. The Bodhisattva said: 'Very good. It is so.'
[Which all sentient beings likewise possess.]
This wondrously clear enlightened mind all sentient beings likewise possess; only they are deluded and do not reveal it.

blocks.text: 1. The Method of Upholding Sutras and Mantras

inline.s: [Someone
(a person)
asked about the method of upholding sutras and mantras. The Bodhisattva said: 'What is called upholding sutras and mantras is to uphold one's own mind. The essential point is to
(the key is to)

directly clarify the mind-ground. If one merely says he has become familiar with the recitation and chanted a great deal, and again recites such-and-such a sutra, mantra, or Buddha, thinking he has great merit, yet cannot dissolve every sentence back into his own nature, nor deeply understand the Buddha's wonderful truth
(the exquisite and true principle)

, and thinks he can thereby attain the fruit — have you not seen those at the crossroads: the eyeless, the footless, the female beggar, the male beggar, who all day long never stop their mouths, reciting from morning to night? Count their recitations — in one year, is it not
(in a single year, does it exceed)
several hundred thousand times? And in the end they are
(in the end, still)

the crippled and the beggars, never having realized so much as a hair's breadth of fruit. Why is this? Only because they have no understanding and no practice. Therefore know: when you uphold this scripture, you should practice in accordance with it. And further you should make great vows: either to seek rebirth in the Buddha-land, or to seek to clarify the mind-ground, or to arouse great wisdom, or to benefit and save sentient beings. All these rely on the Tathāgata's vast, far-reaching power, so as to accomplish the practitioner's vows. Only in this way is it the upholding of sutras, the upholding of mantras, and the reciting of the Buddha's name.']

Someone asked about the method of upholding sutras and mantras. The Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing said: 'What is called upholding sutras and mantras is to uphold one's own mind, bringing it into accord with the sutra and the mantra; the key is to directly clarify the mind-ground. If one merely says he has become familiar with the recitation and chanted a great deal, and again recites such-and-such a sutra, mantra, or Buddha, thinking that he thereby has great merit, yet cannot dissolve every sentence back into his own nature, nor deeply understand the Buddha's exquisite and true principle, and so says he can gain merit — have you not seen those at the crossroads, the eyeless and footless cripples, the male and female beggars, who all day long never stop their mouths, reciting from morning to night? In a year, does their recitation not exceed several hundred thousand times? And in the end they are still the crippled and the beggars, having never realized so much as a hair's breadth of merit. Why is this? Only because they have no understanding and no practice. Therefore know: when you uphold this scripture, you should practice in accordance with it. And further you should make great vows: either to seek rebirth in the Buddha-land, or to seek to clarify the mind-ground, or to arouse great wisdom, or to benefit and save sentient beings. And all these vows rely on the Tathāgata's vast, far-reaching power, granting strength to the practitioner, and only then do they come to fulfillment. Only in this way is it the upholding of sutras, the upholding of mantras, and the reciting of the Buddha's name.'
Here the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing reveals the methods of holding the sutra, holding the mantra, and reciting the Buddha's name:
Directly illuminate the mind-ground; dissolve everything back into self-nature, and cultivate as taught.

[As for holding the sutra and mantra] Holding the sutra and mantra is to hold one's own mind, causing it to correspond to the sutra and mantra. So the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing thereupon revealed:
“The essential
is
(the key is)
to directly illuminate the mind-ground,”
“every phrase should dissolve back into self-nature,”
“therefore, knowing this, when you hold this sutra, you should immediately cultivate in accordance with this sutra
(cultivating as it teaches)

. [Mind-ground] The mind is the root of all dharmas and can give rise to all dharmas, so the mind is called the 'mind-ground.' Also, because practitioners act in accordance with the mind, the mind is called the 'mind-ground.' [Directly illuminate the mind-ground] Directly strip away the deluded thoughts and greed, hatred, and delusion within the mind, causing the mind to return to clarity. [Every phrase dissolves back into self-nature] Every phrase is carried out upon one's own mind and conduct, causing self-nature to turn from delusion to awareness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is sentient beings; when self-nature is aware, that is the Buddha.”
(See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha
article.)

blocks.text: Entering the Mountain to Await Death

inline.s: [The old monk Tianran, because of a long illness that would not heal, wished to enter Jingshan to await death, so as to leave his bones in the Putong stupa. The Bodhisattva said: 'You wish to live in the mountain awaiting death — this is courting trouble where there is none! Are you worrying that your few old bones have nowhere to be put? You do not know that once the eyes' light falls to the ground
(a person's death)
, and the two legs stretch straight out, then let them hack and chop you with knife and axe
zhuó,
to cut and hack with a knife or an axe)
, burn you with fire and soak you in water — all of it is unrelated to you
(all of it is unrelated to you)
, yet you still make long-term plans for it — this is too foolish. Moreover, this body while alive is already of no benefit; how much the more after death!']

The old monk Tianran, because of a long illness that would not heal, planned to enter Jingshan to await death, so as to place his remains in the Putong stupa. The Bodhisattva said: 'You wish to live in the mountain awaiting death — this is looking for trouble where there is none! Are you still worrying that your few old bones have nowhere to settle? You do not know that once the eyes close and the two feet stretch straight out, and the consciousness (self-nature) has departed, then let them hack and chop you with knife and axe, burn you with fire and soak you in water — it is all unrelated to you; yet you still make long-term plans for it, and this is too foolish. Moreover, this body while alive is already of no benefit — how much the more after death?'

[You should now simplify and set aside all the various matters, and single-mindedly hold the single phrase 'Amitābha Buddha,' never casting it aside for a single thought-moment; then Amitābha Buddha will be your good companion. When the great limit
(the time of death)
arrives, he will appear in person to guide you, and you will be reborn in Ultimate Bliss — how is this not superior
(how is this not better)
to entering the mountain to await death? Moreover,
(and furthermore)

birth, aging, sickness, and death are the unavoidable sorrows of this world. Since you have long been ill, do not concern yourself with whether it heals or not; just have one thought, one mind — whether you live, let it be; whether you die, let it be.']

You should now set aside all those superfluous matters, concentrate your energy on holding the single phrase 'Amitābha Buddha,' never casting it aside for a single thought-moment; then Amitābha Buddha will be your good companion. When the great limit (the time of death) arrives, he will appear in person to guide your consciousness, and you will be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — how is this not better than entering the mountain to await death? Moreover, birth, aging, sickness, and death are the unavoidable sorrows of this world. Though you have long been ill, do not concern yourself with whether it heals or not; just be single-mindedly devoted to the one Buddha-name — whether you live, let it be; whether you die, let it be.'
Rather than passively entering the mountain to await death, it is better to actively recite the Buddha and seek rebirth — this is the choice of wisdom!
[Jingshan] Located about
kilometers northwest of Hangzhou, it is one of the five mountains of the world and enjoys great renown in Buddhism. [Putong stupa]
A stupa that gathers in one place the bones of deceased monks, and so is called the Putong (universal) stupa.

blocks.text: Submitting to a Teacher and Receiving the Precepts

inline.s: [The monk Bu'er was about to submit to a teacher and receive the precepts. The Bodhisattva said: 'What a pity! What a pity! With such an imposing appearance and such a fine bearing, you do not know how to reflect on yourself. Examining what you do, you are no different from an ordinary person. I see your body here, yet your spirit already wanders in hell! You must urgently apply yourself to austere self-cultivation and reflection, cut off evil and follow good, seek above the Buddha-fruit and guide below the multitudes of beings. Do not remain muddled and dim, squandering this limited time and bringing upon yourself the burden of ten thousand kalpas.']

The monk Bu'er was about to submit to a teacher and receive the precepts. The Bodhisattva said to him: 'What a pity! What a pity! With such an imposing appearance and such fine bearing, you yet do not know how to reflect on yourself. Examining your actions, you are no different from an ordinary person. I see your body here, yet you have already wandered in spirit to hell! You must urgently apply yourself to austere self-cultivation and reflection, cut off evil and follow good, seek above the Buddha-fruit and guide below the multitudes of beings. Do not remain muddled and dim, losing this limited time and bringing upon yourself the calamity of ten thousand kalpas.'
[As for
(as to)

the matter of receiving the precepts — if you do not receive them, then fine; but once you receive them, you must not transgress them in the slightest. You must guard them purely, like a white jade or a bright pearl, without the least flaw — only then does the precept-character attain fulfillment. For
(this is because)

the precepts are the fundamental entrance to the path for the Buddhas of the three times; do not treat them as child's play! Moreover, if you dwell in stillness or travel in search of masters, you should the more draw near good friends and distance yourself from the mediocre and inferior. Drawing near the good, the path is easy to accomplish; drawing near the evil, the precept-conduct is easy to lose. These two sayings are the essentials of a lifetime of studying the Way — be careful! Remember them!']

As for the matter of receiving the precepts — if you do not receive them, then it is fine; but once you have received them, you must not transgress them in the slightest. You must guard them purely, like a white jade or a bright pearl, without the least flaw, and only then can the precept-character be fulfilled. For the precepts are the fundamental entrance to the path for the Buddhas of the three times, and are no child's play! If you dwell in stillness in one place, or travel in search of masters, you should the more draw near good friends and distance yourself from those vulgar and inferior. Drawing near the good, the path is easy to accomplish; drawing near the evil, the precept-conduct is easy to lose. These two sayings (drawing near the good, the path is easy to accomplish; drawing near the evil, the precept-conduct is easy to lose) are the essential formulas of a lifetime of studying the Way — you must earnestly put them into practice and keep them in mind!'
For a cultivator, distancing himself from evil and drawing near the good is of utmost importance.
[Self-cultivation] To temper and develop one's moral character. [Flaw (
xiá diàn
A spot or crack in jade, a metaphor for a shortcoming or fault.
[The brothers Ma Yongxi, in a former life,
(a previous life)

were hunters. One day they entered the mountain and together killed a deer, and so were to receive the retribution of a short life. They also once saw the Buddha image in a stupa fall to the ground; they set it up on its seat, bowed, and left. Because of this wholesome cause, they again obtained a human body. The Bodhisattva first gave Yongxi instruction. Yongxi was afraid and sought the way
(longevity)
of a long life.']

The brothers Ma Yongxi, in a former life, were hunters. One day they entered the mountain and together killed a deer, and were to receive the retribution of a short life. They also once saw a Buddha image in a stupa lying on the ground; they set it up on its seat, bowed, and left. Because of this wholesome cause, they again obtained a human body. The Bodhisattva first gave Yongxi instruction. When Yongxi heard it, he was greatly frightened and sought from the Bodhisattva the way of longevity.

[The Bodhisattva said: 'In the past, at the Miaojue Temple in the north, there was a young novice, sixteen years old. There was a physiognomist who could tell of a person's life and death without the slightest error. He said to the novice: "In the last month of autumn of your eighteenth year
(the last month of autumn, the ninth month of the lunar calendar)
, you will die." The novice was greatly afraid. At night he prayed to the Buddha, wishing that from the canon
(the great Buddhist canon)

a sutra might be bestowed upon him, which he would hold for life, to pray for longevity. When he had spoken, he wept beyond endurance, bowed again, and rose. From the great canon he picked up at random the Prajna Sutra of the Diamond
(that is, the Diamond Sutra, whose full title is the Diamond Prajna-paramita Sutra)

. He then copied it and held it, without relaxation day or night. He also kept the precepts with strict purity and came to comprehend the profound principle. Before he was forty, his way of truth spread and flowed, and the four assemblies revered and looked up to him. Later he lived to eighty and passed away sitting upright. This was the Chan Master Weixing of Luoyang. It was a matter of the sixth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang, and I saw it myself.']

The Bodhisattva said: 'In the past, at the Miaojue Temple in the north, there was a young novice, sixteen years old. There was a physiognomist who could tell of a person's life and death without the slightest error. He said to the novice: "In the ninth month of your eighteenth year, you will die." The novice was greatly afraid. At night he prayed to the Buddha, wishing that from the great canon a single sutra might be bestowed upon him, which he would hold for life, to pray for longevity. When he had spoken, he wept beyond endurance, bowed again, and rose. From the great canon he picked up at random the Diamond Sutra. He then copied it and held it, without relaxation day or night, and also kept the precepts with strict purity, coming to comprehend the profound principle. Before he was forty, his way of truth spread and flowed, and the four assemblies revered and looked up to him. Later he lived to eighty and passed away sitting upright at ease. This was the Chan Master Weixing of Luoyang. It was a matter of the sixth year of the Kaiyuan era of Tang Emperor Xuanzong (
), and I saw it with my own eyes.'
[The four assemblies] Bhikshus, bhikshunis, upasakas, and upasikas.
[Bhikshu, bhikshuni]

Those who have left home and received the full precepts. The man is called a bhikshu, the woman a bhikshuni. [Upasaka] Translated into Chinese as the 'pure faithful man'; that is, a male lay disciple who in the world draws near and serves the Three Jewels and upholds the five precepts. [Upasika] Translated into Chinese as the 'pure woman'; that is, a female lay disciple who draws near and serves the Three Jewels and upholds the five precepts.

['Since you now fear a short life and seek a long life, you should, in accordance with this novice, obtain a good copy of the Diamond Sutra, set your mind on copying it, diligently recite it, and further seek to understand its purport — this is inner merit. From today onward, you must not again kill living beings; you should love them as your own body, and also accumulate much hidden virtue — this is outer merit. When both inner and outer are cultivated, the merit is very great; you can naturally unite with Heaven, and the principle of the non-duality of untimely death and long life is established — why worry that your years will not be long? Yet you must be careful to the end as at the beginning; like that novice, without remiss even at eighty, only then does one conform to the Way. Do not in any case have a head without a tail, or practice for ten days and half a month, one or two years, and then drop it. If you indeed reverently follow for your whole life
(without the slightest interruption)
, and your request is not fulfilled, then all the Buddhas and I will both have fallen into false speech.']

Since you now fear a short life and seek a long life, you should, in accordance with this novice, obtain a good copy of the Diamond Sutra (a copy whose text is clear and correct), set your mind on copying it (copying sutras was an important means of spreading the Dharma at that time), diligently practice and recite it, and further seek to understand its meaning — this is inner merit. From today onward, you must not kill any living being again, but should love life as your own body, and also accumulate much hidden virtue — this is outer merit. When both inner and outer are cultivated, the merit is very great; you can naturally unite with Heaven, and the principle of the non-duality of short life and long life is established — why worry that your life-span will not be long? Yet you must, from beginning to end, carefully practice both inner and outer, like that novice who was never remiss even at eighty; only then do you conform to the Way of Heaven. Do not in any case have a beginning without an end, or practice ten days and half a month, one year or two, and then throw it away. If indeed you reverently follow it for your whole bodily life, without interruption, and yet your request is not fulfilled, then all the Buddhas and I will both have fallen into false speech.'”

[Hidden virtue] Good (beneficial) deeds done for others in secret. [The non-duality of short life and long life] Whether one's life-span is short or long, it never changes. This saying comes from the Mencius

Jin Xin (I). The original text reads: 'Mencius said: One who exhausts his mind knows his nature. Knowing his nature, he knows Heaven. To preserve his mind and nourish his nature is how he serves Heaven. Whether one dies young or lives long, one never changes; cultivating oneself and awaiting (
sì

waiting for) it, this is how one establishes his destiny.' (The meaning of this passage: to exhaust one's loving-kindness of mind is to awaken to one's own original nature. Having awakened to one's own original nature, one knows Heaven. One should preserve one's benevolent mind and nourish one's own nature, and in this way serve Heaven. Whether one's life is short or long, it never changes; one merely cultivates oneself and nurtures one's nature to await Heaven's decree — this is how one shapes one's own destiny!) [Exhausting the body] To exhaust one's bodily life; to exhaust this life's form and life-span.

blocks.text: Holding the Resolve Over the Long Term

inline.s: [The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Dingzhuan
zhuān
the same as 'zhuan' — single-minded)

saying: 'It is most rare and difficult for you father and son to practice my teachings. But you must hold your resolve over the long term, and must not give rise to thoughts seeking a spiritual response. The two words "cultivation" should be practiced like the daily affairs of putting on clothes and eating rice — only then is it right.']
The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Dingzhuan (
zhuān

the same as 'zhuan' — single-minded): 'It is most rare and difficult for you father and son to practice my teachings. But you must arouse a long-term resolve, and must not give rise to thoughts seeking a spiritual response. The two words "cultivation" should be practiced until they are as indispensable as putting on clothes and eating rice in daily life.'
[Holding the resolve over the long term] The resolve to practice my teaching, enduring without change. [The long-term resolve] A heart that endures without change.

[The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dinghong's mother, saying: 'In the past you had a thought of seeking the Way, but you did not encounter a person of right understanding — this is deeply to be pitied. Now I shall give you clear instruction. In the past, when you were a bhikshu, you vigorously exerted yourself in practice, without relaxation day or night. Because your mind was fierce, in calm stillness a view suddenly arose: "Why can I not quickly attain Buddhahood?" Another day, hearing the words "The Buddhas are without marks; this very mind is the Buddha," you increased your wrong thought, saying: "Since all dharmas are empty and still, and my mind is the Buddha, what need is there to practice?" But you do not know that this is the ultimate emptiness-principle, and not something easily spoken of by one newly entering the Dharma-realm.']

The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dinghong's mother, saying: 'In the past you had a thought of seeking the Way, but you did not meet a true good friend — this is deeply to be pitied. Now I shall give you clear instruction. In the past, when you were a bhikshu, you vigorously exerted yourself in practice, without resting day or night. Because your mind's actions were fierce, in calm stillness a view suddenly arose: "Why can I not quickly attain Buddhahood?" Another day, hearing the words "The Buddhas are without marks; this very mind is the Buddha," you further increased your wrong thought, saying to yourself: "Since all dharmas are empty and still, and my mind is the Buddha, what need is there to practice?" But you do not know that this is the ultimate emptiness-principle, whose subtle meaning is not something a beginner can easily fathom.'

[From this the bhikshu fell into wrong views and no longer advanced in practice. He himself thought he had realized the great Way, and so went from delusion into delusion, sunk in the long night. Pity the beings! Seeking the Way without encountering a true good friend, one cannot but fall into the snare — how can one not be careful! Now you should know that, because of the wrong view of the past, you obtained the retribution of the five outflows
Because you lost right knowledge, you again met an evil teacher, whose poison-sting
shì
you personally suffered — how can you not arouse fear? Now you should quickly arouse right faith, and with all your mind remember Amitābha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.']

From this the bhikshu fell into wrong views and no longer advanced in practice. He thought he had already realized the great Way, and so went from delusion into delusion, sunk in the long night. How pitiable are beings! Seeking the Way without encountering a true good friend, one cannot but fall into the snare of wrong views — how can one not be vigilant! Now you should know that, owing to the wrong view of the past, you felt the retribution of transmigrating through the five paths. Because you lost right knowledge, you again met an evil teacher and personally suffered his poison-harming — how can you not arouse fear? Now you should quickly arouse right faith, and with all your mind think on Amitābha Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.'

[The five outflows] Here it refers to the five paths that have outflows. 'Outflow' is another name for afflictions. [The five paths] These are the places where afflicted beings come and go, hence called 'paths.' There are five: one, the hell path; two, the hungry-ghost path; three, the animal path; four, the human path; five, the heaven path.
Question: Since 'all dharmas are empty and still, and my mind is the Buddha,' what need is there to practice?
Answer: 'All dharmas are empty and still' means that all dharmas are empty of anything at all, still without arising or ceasing. The whole ten Dharma-realms are a single dream of ignorance
(see
The Real Nature of All Dharmas
article)

, so all dharmas are illusions, empty of anything at all, still without arising or ceasing. 'My mind is the Buddha' is what is commonly called 'this very mind is the Buddha.' Here 'mind' refers to self-nature, while the 'mind' of body-and-mind refers to the function of self-nature. The meaning of 'this very mind is the Buddha' is: the Buddha is nothing other than the mind (self-nature). And in essence, the self-nature of the Buddhas and the self-nature of sentient beings are entirely the same; only, the Buddhas' self-nature is aware, while sentient beings' self-nature is deluded.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: 'When self-nature is deluded, that is sentient beings; when self-nature is aware, that is the Buddha.' (See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha

article.) Practice is meant to turn self-nature from delusion to awareness, from sentient being to Buddha. Therefore one must practice in order to leave the cycle of rebirth and to realize Buddhahood.
[The ten Dharma-realms]
Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary; the last four are the four noble.

[Wu Xiu asked on behalf of a friend how long his life would be. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse, saying: 'Human life is like the morning dew, floating and unsettled, with no fixed time; unable to escape the dream and illusion, why must one seek to know beforehand?' He further revealed: 'Do not for him ask the date; when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you may be sure he will be in a fluster.' This friend indeed died of illness on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the following year. When Wu Xiu heard this, he sought instruction.]

Wu Xiu asked on behalf of a friend how long his life-span would be. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse: 'Human life is like the morning dew, floating and unsettled, with no fixed time; unable to escape the dream and illusion, why must one seek to know beforehand?' He further revealed: 'Do not for him ask the date of his death; when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month comes, be sure he will be in a fluster.' This friend indeed fell ill and died on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the following year. When Wu Xiu heard this news, he sought instruction from the Bodhisattva.

[The Bodhisattva said: 'Yuan Bo, you should know that studying the Way without understanding this mind is like building a house without a foundation, or crossing a river without a raft. One who wishes to understand the mind should minutely investigate: this body and this mind — from what do they arise? Since the four great elements are illusory, where is the mind to be lodged? Body and mind being illusory, the world and its dust-particles are without the slightest difference. The myriad dharmas before one's eyes — from where do they arise? From where do they cease? If there is no arising and ceasing, then the illuminating and that which is illuminated both have nothing to rely on, and of itself one sees the ground of True Thusness' extinction and peace.']

The Bodhisattva said: 'Yuan Bo, you should know that studying the Way without understanding this mind is like building a house without a foundation, or crossing a river without a boat. To understand the mind, you must minutely investigate: this body and this mind — from what do they arise? Since the four great elements (here referring to the body) are illusory, on what will the mind rely? Therefore the mind too is illusory. Having understood that body and mind are illusory, then the whole world and a single particle of dust are without the slightest difference, for they are all illusions. Then, further contemplate: the myriad dharmas before one's eyes — from where do they arise? To where do they pass away? If they are without arising and ceasing (illusions naturally have no arising or ceasing), then the illuminating and the illuminated both have nothing to rely on, and of itself one will see the ground of True Thusness' extinction and peace, directly realizing that birth and death are illusory.'
[The four great elements]

The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. Earth has the nature of hardness, water of moisture, fire of warmth, and wind of motion. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures — hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion — and so they are called 'great.' For example, the hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, flesh, and sinews of a human body are the hard earth element; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, phlegm, tears, urine, and excrement are the moist water element; warmth and heat are the warm fire element; and the in-and-out of one breath is the moving wind element.

[Where is the mind to be lodged?] Here 'mind' refers to the shadows of the six sense-objects. [The shadows of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced by the six senses conditioning on the six sense-objects, and these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, hence they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantom images of conditioning on the six sense-objects. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: 'What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time, all beings have all manner of inversion, like a person who is lost and mistakes the four directions; falsely taking the four great elements as their own form, and the shadows of the six sense-objects as their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; the sick one falsely grasps them. Because of this false grasping, not only is he deluded about the self-nature of this sky, but he is also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this there is falsely the transmigration of birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.' (Translation: What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time, all beings have had all manner of inversion, taking the false as real, and this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his way, mistaking north for south and east for west; falsely taking the body formed of the four great elements as the substance of self, and the thoughts arising from the six senses conditioning on the six sense-objects as the substance of mind. It is like eyes that are dazzled, falsely seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; these are phantoms falsely grasped by a diseased eye. Because of false grasping, one not only falsely grasps the emptiness of the sky as real, but also thinks real flowers truly arise from it. Because beings, through the inversion and delusion of not comprehending, falsely take the illusory body and mind as real and cling to them as self, they thereupon transmigrate in birth and death, and so this is called ignorance.)

[Kong Sheng of Gouqu had kept a vegetarian diet for twenty years. Thinking of his own aging, he asked: 'What is there after death?' And wept without cease. The Bodhisattva said: 'You need not shed sorrowful tears; just follow what I say, deeply believe and practice it, and after death you will naturally have a good place to settle your body.' Thereupon he bestowed a verse: 'In the West there is a Pure Land, where humans and devas alike take refuge; if you can cultivate this gate, secure
(the same as 'wen' — still and secure)
without fear or doubt.']

Kong Sheng of Gouqu had maintained a vegetarian diet for twenty years. Thinking of his own aging, he asked the Bodhisattva: 'What will there be after death?' Thereupon he wept without cease. The Bodhisattva instructed: 'You need not weep in sorrow; only follow what I say, deeply believe and practice it, and after your life ends you will naturally have a good place to dwell.' Thereupon he gave him a verse: 'In the West there is a Pure Land, where humans and devas alike take refuge; if you can cultivate this gate, secure and at peace, without fear or doubt.'

[Shen Wenzhou was celebrated for his mastery of cold-damage, and had just arrived to pay respects. The Bodhisattva asked: 'When cold enters the pericardium, what illness is that?' He answered: 'It is called cold-stroke
zhòng hán,
illness caused by catching cold)

.' Thereupon, as an illustration for the assembly, he said: 'You only know that when cold enters the pericardium, it is called the illness of cold-stroke. But if a wrong enters the mind, that is an illness that costs one his life! You people take only a bodily illness as an illness and promptly regulate and cure it; yet when the mind has a great illness, you do not consult a bright physician, do not seek a wondrous medicine, and let it suffer its pain without awareness — alas!']

Shen Wenzhou was a master proficient in the Treatise on Cold-Damage, and had just arrived to pay respects to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva asked: 'When cold enters the pericardium, what illness is that?' Shen Wenzhou answered: 'This is cold-stroke (
zhòng hán

, illness caused by catching cold).' Thereupon the Bodhisattva instructed the assembly: 'You only know that when cold enters the pericardium, one gets the illness of cold-stroke. But if a wrong enters the mind, that is a fatal illness! You people take only a bodily illness as an illness and immediately regulate and cure it; but when the mind has a great illness, you do not consult a bright physician, do not seek a wondrous medicine, and let it suffer its pain without awareness — how sorrowful!'

[Treatise on Cold-Damage] The earliest work in existing Chinese medicine that systematically discusses externally-contracted disease. Ten volumes in all. Written by Zhang Zhongjing of the Eastern Han in the

rd century. It established the six-channel syndrome differentiation and principles of treatment, and the combination of prescriptions; in diagnosis it threads together the four examinations and the eight guiding principles.

[Chen Daxin followed the teaching and recited the Buddha's name with the utmost sincerity. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse, saying: 'In the pool of the eight virtues a lotus has already been planted; indeed a single thought is most profound and deep. Though its watering and nurture rely on the Tathagata's power, its growth depends entirely on a mind of resolve.' He further addressed the assembly: 'In this land, when one makes the vow to be reborn, then in that land a lotus immediately grows. Therefore he spoke thus; you should arouse deep faith.']

Chen Daxin followed the Bodhisattva's teaching and recited the Buddha's name with the utmost sincerity. The Bodhisattva revealed a verse: 'In the pool of the eight virtues (the pool filled with the water of the eight virtues) a lotus has already been planted; indeed a single thought is most profound and deep. Though its watering and nurture rely on the Tathagata's power, its growth depends entirely on a mind of resolve.' He further instructed the assembly: 'In this land, the moment one makes the vow to be reborn, in that land (the Land of Ultimate Bliss) a lotus at once grows. So my verse says "in the pool of the eight virtues a lotus has already been planted"; you should arouse deep faith.'

[The water of the eight virtues] In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is a pool of the seven jewels, filled with the water of the eight virtues. This water has eight kinds of supreme virtue: one, pure and clear; two, cool and refreshing; three, sweet and fine; four, light and soft; five, moistening and enriching; six, peaceful and harmonious; seven, when drunk, it removes thirst, hunger, and countless other ills; eight, after drinking, it is certain to nourish the faculties and the four great elements, and to increase all manner of supreme wholesome roots.

blocks.text: Fond of the Art of Elixir

inline.s: [Sun Zhongbai was fond of the art of elixir; after long practice it was ineffective, so he came to the gathering to pay respects. The Bodhisattva rebuked him, saying: 'Old baldhead, today you have changed this look to come see me? Let me ask you: when can your gold elixir be completed?' He answered: 'I am precisely seeking its completion.' The Bodhisattva said: 'If it is completed, be sure to keep several pellets; do not eat them all into your belly. Wait until
sì
wait)
you see old Yama, so that you may make a gift to present. Foolish old man, this matter truly has no share for you; it is better to return to what you ought to do.' Sun bowed and thanked him.']

Sun Zhongbai was fond of the art of alchemy; after long practice it proved ineffective, so he came to the gathering and paid respects to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva rebuked him: 'Old baldhead, today you have changed your visage to see me? Let me ask you: when can your gold elixir be completed?' Sun Zhongbai answered: 'I have precisely come to ask you to help me complete it.' The Bodhisattva said: 'If it is completed, be sure to keep several pellets; do not swallow them all into your belly. When you meet old Yama, you can use them as a gift to present to him, begging him to spare you. Foolish old man, the matter of refining the elixir and becoming an immortal surely has no share for you; it is better to do what you ought to do (the task that falls within your proper lot).' Sun Zhongbai bowed and thanked the Bodhisattva for his instruction.
[The art of elixir]

It includes both the 'external elixir' and the 'internal elixir.' The external elixir uses cinnabar (red mercuric sulfide) along with lead, sulfur, and other ingredients, refined into a yellow medicinal gold whose product is called the gold elixir. Daoism holds that after taking it one can become a transcendent and never age. The gold elixir mostly refers to the external elixir, but also to the internal elixir that one refines — taking the body as a 'furnace and vessel,' using the 'essence' and 'breath' within the body as the medicine, and refining by means of 'spirit.' Daoism holds that causing essence, breath, and spirit to congeal can form a 'holy embryo,' whereby one can shed the body and be reborn as a transcendent.
[Gifts]
Presents intended as offerings.

[After a while, the Bodhisattva again said: 'Foolish old man, do you know your own proper lot?' He answered: 'Seeking to see my nature is my proper lot.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Do you know this nature — is it great or small, blue or yellow?' He answered: 'Nature has no such marks.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Then where do you wish to seek to see it?' Sun had no reply, and so aroused faith and took refuge, wishing to be a disciple and asking for a Dharma name. Thereupon he revealed a verse for him, saying: 'Nature has no marks of great or small, blue or yellow; how can there be a name for you to call? If one does not reach the profound mystery of this, every word and half a phrase is confusion.']

After a while, the Bodhisattva again said: 'Foolish old man, do you know your own proper lot?' Sun Zhongbai answered: 'I seek to see my nature; this is my proper lot.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Do you know this nature — is it great or small (in form), blue or yellow (in color)?' Sun Zhongbai answered: 'Nature has no such marks.' The Bodhisattva said: 'Since it has no marks, then where do you wish to seek to see it?' Sun Zhongbai could not answer, and so aroused faith and took refuge in the Bodhisattva, wishing to be his disciple and asking him to bestow a Dharma name. Thereupon the Bodhisattva revealed a verse: 'Nature has no marks of great or small, blue or yellow; how can there be a name for you to call? If one does not reach the profound mystery of this, every word and half a phrase is confusion (a mistake).'

['I now forcibly establish a name for you; you may be called Da Ben. After this, your remaining time will not amount to seven or eight years — do not squander the thirty-six years of ascetic practice of eight hundred years ago!' Sun then asked how this body would come to an end. The Bodhisattva said: 'An end is an end; why ask again how it will end?' Sun then asked how to practice. The Bodhisattva said: 'The gate of the Pure Land can broadly gather beings of all types. You ask about practice — you should be mindful of Amitābha Buddha, make the vow to be reborn there, then all will be settled once and for all; be no more deluded.']

I now give you the name Da Ben. After this, your life-span will not exceed seven or eight years; do not in any way squander the thirty-six years of ascetic practice of eight hundred years ago!' Sun Zhongbai thereupon asked how this body would come to an end. The Bodhisattva said: 'An end is an end; why ask moreover how it will end?' Sun Zhongbai then asked: 'How should one practice?' The Bodhisattva said: 'The gate of the Pure Land can broadly gather beings of all faculties. You ask about practice — you should be mindful of Amitābha Buddha and make the vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and then you will have everything settled once and for all; be deluded no longer.'
[I forcibly establish a name for you] Dharms are originally without name, so to establish this name is called 'forcibly doing so.'

[Then all is settled once and for all] Sun Zhongbai's goal was to see his nature and attain awakening; the Bodhisattva taught him to recite the Buddha, because 'once one sees Amitābha, why worry about not awakening?' Hence he said: 'then one settles everything once and for all.'
The Bodhisattva further admonished the assembly, saying: “Since ancient times the great sages and great worthies, in explaining the subtle
(elucidating the subtle principle)
and establishing the teaching
(carrying on the work of conversion)

, have been entirely refined and entirely simple. Persons of superior faculty, hearing, awaken; those of middling and inferior faculty, hearing, cultivate; all return to the great Way. But the various writings that came after them busied themselves with verbosity and esoteric talk, so that ordinary folk puzzled over them and formed views, until error was passed on as truth and they sank deep into the perverse
Clutching their darkness while life passed
(clutching these perverse and muddled views until death)
, they were not even aware of it.”

The Bodhisattva further guided the assembly, saying: “Since ancient times, the great sages and great worthies, in elucidating the wonderful principle and carrying on the work of teaching, have been wholly refined and wholly simple. Persons of superior faculty (those of the highest capacity), hearing, awaken; those of middling and inferior faculty, hearing, cultivate; all return to the great Way. But the various writings that came after them, however, devoted themselves to verbosity (stringing together chapter after chapter of stuff) and dark sayings (deliberately mystifying), so that ordinary folk would puzzle over them and form views (puzzling over their doctrines and so forming their own opinions), until error was passed on as truth and they sank deep into the perverse and the eccentric (deviation from the right is called perverse; straying from the center is called eccentric). Thus they clutched to these perverse, muddled views for a lifetime, and were not themselves even aware of it.”

[Wording it into a discourse] The Buddhas and the great patriarchs, the venerable masters, truly recounted the states they had realized and their own experience, exactly as the book says of one who has gone to Yanjing: he tells others how to walk the road, and they are able to reach Yanjing; everything is refined and simple. But from ancient times there have also been not a few who sought fame and reputation (people who had never been to Yanjing), who dug a piece here from the sutras and treatises, picked a bit over there, and then arbitrarily strung it together and embellished it, making grand theses, until fish-eyes were passed off as pearls and true and false became hard to tell. Many deceived students, following these in practice, though they toiled diligently, went in exactly the opposite direction; the more they cultivated, the more deluded they became, afflictions sprouted on every side, they clutched their darkness through life, and wasted their years. Therefore, when reading these “great works,” one should first examine whether their content agrees with the sutras and treatises, and whether their author has genuine power and attainment in practice; only then will one not be led astray. Master Honen’s fishing in troubled waters is a bitter warning of exactly this sort (see
Master Honen’s Forging of the Great Vow Gate
[Such as Daben: because he read the Can Tong
(the Can Tong Qi)
and the Wu Zhen
(the Wu Zhen Pian)
and other books, but did not know the essential teaching, he falsely trusted
(believed recklessly)
the erroneous transmission, thought he had attained, clutched it fondly
(deluded attachment and clinging)

would not let it go. To white hair he had no accomplishment, and various afflictions arose. The Bodhisattva said, these are truly to be pitied. Therefore, since you now recognize your former error, you should reverence right faith.”]
