For example, Daben, because he read the Can Tong Qi, the Wu Zhen Pian, and other such books, did not know the true essential teaching, but falsely believed the erroneous transmission, thinking he had some attainment, and clung to it fondly, unable to let it go. As a result, to white hair he had no accomplishment, and afflictions sprouted on every side. The Bodhisattva said: these misled beings are truly pitiable! Therefore, since you have now recognized your former error, you ought to reverence right faith.”
[At one time, the Bodhisattva was about to come to the Dharma assembly. Eight disciples — Wuxiu, Changshe, Changyuan, Dingmao, Daben, Zha Dinghong, Chen Dingzhuan, and Zha Dingmin — reverently gazing
yóng
, the look of admiring reverence)
stood
zhù
, standing for a long time)
, and together chanted the Buddha’s name. Suddenly a wondrous fragrance came from the sky; all were delighted and had never known such a thing.]

At one time, the Bodhisattva was about to come to the Dharma assembly, and eight disciples — Wuxiu, Changshe, Changyuan, Dingmao, Daben, Zha Dinghong, Chen Dingzhuan, and Zha Dingmin — stood reverently and chanted the Buddha’s name together. Suddenly a wondrous fragrance came from the sky, and the whole assembly was greatly delighted, having never experienced such a thing.

[The Bodhisattva said: “Excellent! Excellent! Do you know that this assembly today has a condition from past lives? In the sixth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, I left home at the Jingyin Temple in the eastern capital of the Northern Wei, as a great bhikshu. Because of the turmoil of war I journeyed south, and took up my staff at the foot of Jiming Mountain
(the mountain’s foot)

. At that time, you eight relied on me in study and practice, but before long the war scattered us each on our way. Two years after that I passed away at Tianzhu in Wulin. Later, in the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang, I was the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe, and likewise abandoned rank to leave home. Now you eight, gathered together to recite the Buddha’s name, also came about through my stirring the resolve, exactly as in former times. But since you eight left me, more than eight hundred years have passed, and you are still drifting without return — truly pitiable, truly painful! Now for you I shall again set forth clearly the practice you have cultivated, that you may quickly accomplish it and soon attain liberation. Each of you should listen attentively.”]
The Bodhisattva said: “Excellent! Excellent! Do you know that this assembly today has a condition from past lives. Formerly, in the sixth year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang (

), I left home at the Jingyin Temple, the eastern capital of the Northern Wei, as a great bhikshu. Because of the turmoil of war I journeyed south and rested my staff at the foot of Jiming Mountain. At that time, you eight relied on me in study and practice, but not long after the war scattered us each apart. Two years later I passed away at Tianzhu in Wulin. Later, in the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang (

), I was the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe, and likewise abandoned my rank to leave home. Now you eight, gathered together to recite the Buddha’s name, also came about through my stirring the resolve, exactly as of old. But since you eight left me, more than eight hundred years have passed, and you are still transmigrating ceaselessly in the six realms — truly pitiable, truly painful! Now for you I shall set forth clearly the path of practice, that you may quickly attain the Way and soon be liberated. Each of you should now concentrate your mind and listen attentively.”
[Resting the staff]
A monk taking up residence in a place. The staff is the khakkhara.
[Passing away]
A term for the death of a Buddha, a Bodhisattva, or an eminent monk. “Passing away” means entering still nirvāṇa; as a manifestation of nirvāṇa, it is not a true extinction.

blocks.text: Diligent Practice of the Pure Karma

inline.s: [Addressing Wuxiu, he said: “Though formerly you pursued the esoteric path, yet you were able to revere the Buddhas; know that this is a condition from former lives. Now you should quickly rouse a deep resolve and diligently practice the pure karma, leading the others in the right way
(that is, to lead and set the example)

. Do not waste these thirteen years that yet remain to you. I give you a verse: Eight hundred years ago was a goodly bond; today we meet, and I point to the blue sky. You know already the mid-autumn moon of this very ground; do not seek a ferryboat upon the long river.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Wuxiu, saying: “Though formerly you pursued the esoteric path, yet you could revere the Buddhas; know that this is a condition from former lives. Now you should quickly arouse a deep resolve and diligently practice the pure karma, leading the assembly to cultivate on the right path. Do not squander the thirteen years of life still left to you! I give you a verse:
Eight hundred years ago, a goodly bond (eight hundred years ago we were master and disciple),
Today we meet, and I point to the blue sky (causing you to see the moon — the true great Way),
You know already the mid-autumn moon of this very ground (a metaphor: since you already know the most appropriate great Way — the Pure Land teaching),
Do not seek a ferryboat upon the long river (then do not go seeking a boat to search out another land’s moon; a metaphor for not seeking any other path of practice).”

[Addressing Changshe, he said: “You always hold the Great Compassion Dharani — how do you hold it?” He replied: “The mantra I hold is distinct and clear; the mind that holds it is entirely ungraspable.” The Bodhisattva said: “To hold it thus is called true holding. I give you a verse: You hold the Great Compassion Mantra; you should know the Great Compassion mind — apart from name and apart from mark, and thereby cross over the multitude of beings.”]

To Changshe he instructed: “You always hold the Great Compassion Dharani — how do you hold it?” Changshe replied: “The mantra I hold is distinct and clear; the mind that holds it is entirely ungraspable.” The Bodhisattva said: “To be able to hold it thus is called true holding. I give you a verse in charge to you: You hold the Great Compassion Mantra; you should know the Great Compassion mind — apart from name and apart from mark, and thereby (uniting compassion and emptiness) cross over the multitude of beings.”
[Addressing Changyuan, he said: “Since you have already left home, you must
(be sure to)

be humble and gentle, reverence and serve your teachers and elders, empty yourself and ask for instruction, and increase your resolve — do not merely sit in the clouds and fog passing your days.” Yuan did not understand
(Changyuan did not comprehend)
. Again he said: “Muddled
mèng méng
, dim and confused)

as you are, can you know your own mind?” Yuan was speechless. So he had him recite the Cundi mantra once, and Yuan recited it accordingly. The Bodhisattva said: “Is this not your mind? What would you call it? A verse: See the firstless, mindless state; this is your original mind. Recite Cundi once, and the whole body is clear.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Changyuan, saying: “Since you have already left home, be sure to be humble and gentle, reverence and serve your teachers and elders, empty yourself and seek instruction, and increase your resolve — do not merely sit in the clouds and fog, muddled, passing your days.” Changyuan did not understand. The Bodhisattva again instructed: “Dim and confused as you are, can you know your own mind?” Changyuan could not answer. (If Changyuan did not even know his own mind, where was he to begin cultivation? So below the Bodhisattva tells him what the mind is.) Thereupon he had Changyuan recite the Cundi mantra once, and Changyuan recited it accordingly. The Bodhisattva said: “Is this not your mind? What would you call it? I give you a verse: See the firstless, mindless state; this is your original mind; recite Cundi once, and the whole body is clear.”
[The Cundi mantra] Namo sadu nan
nā mó sà duō nán
, samyaksambudha
sān miǎo sān pú tuó
koti nan
jù zhī nán,
tadyatha
dá zhí tuō,
om cale cule
ǎn/ōng, zhé lì zhŭ lì,
cundi svaha
zhūn tí suō pó hē.

[This is not your mind — what would you call it?] The mind is the functioning of the self-nature. Changyuan recited the Cundi mantra, and the Bodhisattva immediately said: “Is this not your mind? What would you call it?” Therefore, reciting the mantra is just one’s own mind setting itself to work. Likewise, when one gives rise to confused thoughts, greed, anger, and delusion, it is also one’s own mind setting itself to work. Only, in the former case it is aware, in the latter it is deluded. [See the firstless, mindless state; this is your original mind; recite Cundi once, and the whole body is clear] The meaning of this verse is: seeing the mind that at first is without thought — this is your original mind (no-thought is the original mind; having thought is the consciousness mind); recite the Cundi mantra once, and one should make the mantra within the mind distinct and clear (the whole body clear); if so, one is not sitting in the clouds and fog, muddled, passing one’s days.
[Addressing Dingmao, he said: “You hold the Cundi mantra; in daily life you must apply the mind minutely. Observe all states, whether clamorous or still
(whether noisy or silent)

, whether things or not-things, whether pleasing or repugnant — all are nothing but this mantra manifesting itself, which is my wonderful mind flowing forth at every moment. Holding it thus, you will certainly attain the fruit; and I will also aid you to accomplishment with spiritual power. You should recite my verse: Two lines
(pointing to the Cundi mantra)
of secret, this is your original mind; do not say the Dharma is slight — this Dharma is very deep.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Dingmao, saying: “You hold the Cundi mantra; in daily life you must apply the mind minutely. Observe all states, whether clamorous or still, whether things or not-things, whether pleasing or repugnant — all are nothing but this mantra manifesting itself without being pulled along by the state; this is one’s own wonderful mind flowing forth at every moment. Holding it thus, you will certainly attain the fruit of realization, and I will also aid you to accomplishment with spiritual power. You should recite my verse: Two lines (pointing to the Cundi mantra) of secret, this is your original mind; do not say the Dharma is slight (do not think the Cundi mantra is only two lines of characters) — this Dharma is very deep.”

[Two lines of secret, this is your original mind] The secret of the Cundi mantra lies in holding it until the original mind manifests before you. [This Dharma is very deep] In holding the mantra there are

three barriers: the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, the samadhi manifesting, and the correct samadhi apart from holding. Master Huiming taught: “What is the first barrier? When a practitioner holds the mantra and reaches the point where ten thousand thoughts return to one, no second thought arising, this is called passing the first barrier. But this is pressing down the grass with a stone — not yet the ultimate. What is the second barrier? When the mantra is held to the point of holding without holding, and not holding while holding, and who it is that holds, one does not even know, even as it seems two persons are holding at once — this is called the samadhi manifesting, also called passing the second barrier. What is the third barrier? When the mantra is held to the point where true, false, and Dharma, all three, are unknown, and one enters deep samadhi, attaining the correct samadhi apart from holding — having nothing at all, one realizes the reality-mark, all things complete — this is called passing the third barrier.” (See
Master Huiming’s Recorded Instructions
.) These are also the three barriers of Buddha-recitation, passing from the one mind of practice into the one mind of principle.

[Observe all states, whether clamorous or still, whether things or not-things, whether pleasing or repugnant — all are nothing but this mantra manifesting itself, which is my wonderful mind flowing forth at every moment] The ten thousand dharmas are empty and still; the mantra-body is empty and still; the wonderful mind is empty and still — three and yet one. This is the state of holding the mantra into the reality-mark, the one mind of principle. Because beginning students find it hard to grasp, the text has not been explained in this way; if a practitioner’s work approaches this, there is no need of explanation, and one can of oneself comprehend the Bodhisattva’s instruction. The phrase “two lines of secret, this is your original mind” in the verse below is likewise this situation. Hence Mr. Peng Shaosheng, in his postface, praises it: “Elucidating the wondrous purport of the one mind, exhausting the mystery of the upward-turning gate.”

[He asked Daben: “What will you do?” He replied: “I wish to understand the mind.” The Bodhisattva said: “Is that not empty talk of the mouth? You should diligently recite the Buddha’s name; its merit is tenfold. I also give you a verse: apart from the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your very mind; believe deeply and be not confused; in a single thought, no birth.”]

The Bodhisattva asked Daben: “What do you intend to do?” Daben replied: “I wish to understand the mind and see the nature.” The Bodhisattva said: “Is this not a stock phrase of the mouth? You should diligently recite the Buddha’s name; its merit is tenfold that of your mouth-talk. I give you a verse too: apart from the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your very mind; believe deeply and be not confused; in a single thought, no birth.”
[Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; the Buddha is your very mind] Concerning the principle of “just this mind, just this Buddha,” one may refer to
The Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

[Addressing Zha Dinghong, he said: “You hold the Diamond Prajna; you should know there are seven not-holdings, namely: when the mind is scattered and dull, do not hold; when there has been offense, do not hold; after entering an impure place, do not hold; after drinking wine, do not hold; when disturbed by people and not pure, do not hold; when a matter is about to be done and not yet done, do not hold; when the mind is occupied with other recollection, do not hold. If you are firmly resolved to hold and recite, you should be apart from these seven; and when you have recited to full familiarity, hold it within the contemplative mind. If you can do this, then the merit is inconceivable, and the retribution is inconceivable. The Buddha has a sincere word; you must guard and sustain it. Again I give you a verse: the Prajna sutra — its merit is without end; it pulls up the root of deluded thought, and delivers from the sickness of birth and death.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dinghong, saying: “You hold the Diamond Sutra; you should know there are seven not-holdings, namely: when the mind is scattered and dull, do not hold; when there has been offense, do not hold; after entering an impure place, do not hold; after drinking wine, do not hold; when disturbed by people and not pure, do not hold; when a matter is about to be done and not yet done, do not hold; when the mind is occupied with other recollection, do not hold. If you are firmly resolved to hold and recite, you should be apart from these seven items; and when you have recited to full familiarity, hold it within the contemplative mind. If you can truly do this, then the merit is inconceivable, and the retribution is inconceivable. The Buddha has a sincere word; you must surely guard and sustain it. Again I give you a verse: the Prajna scripture (pointing to the Diamond Sutra) — its merit is without end; it pulls up the root of deluded thought, and delivers from the sickness of birth and death.”
[The Buddha has a sincere word]

The merit and virtue of holding, reciting, and reading the Diamond Sutra are extremely vast, and its retribution is inconceivable; the Buddha speaks of it repeatedly in the Diamond Sutra. For example: “In the future age, if good men and good women are able, with regard to this sutra, to hold, recite, and read it, the Tathagata, with Buddha-wisdom, knows all such persons and sees all such persons, and they will all accomplish immeasurable, boundless merit.” “If a person is able to hold, recite, and read it, and widely proclaim it to others, the Tathagata knows all such persons and sees all such persons, and they will all accomplish merit that is immeasurable, uncountable, without bounds, and inconceivable. Such persons as these will bear the burden of the Tathagata’s anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.” “In the future age, at the end of five hundred years, if there are beings who hear this sutra, believe, understand, accept, and hold it, then such persons are the foremost and most rare.”
[Guard and sustain]

Protection and free flowing, the two stages of removing habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. “Protection” means to take every care of the holy embryo so that it is not harmed; “free flowing” means that after the holy embryo has matured into a full-grown man, it follows the circumstances and conditions and operates of itself, being further tempered amid favorable and adverse conditions.

[Addressing Chen Dingzhuan, he said: “The petty person does evil and only fears that others know; the noble person does good and likewise only fears that others know. You should use the mind of the noble person who is careful in the Way, and do Buddha’s work. Further, there is a verse: do not ask that others know; do not hope for heaven’s response; constantly unify your mind — it must be firm and upright.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Chen Dingzhuan, saying: “The petty person does evil and only fears that others know; the noble person does good and likewise only fears that others know. You should use the mind of the noble person who is careful in the Way, and do Buddha’s work. Further, there is a verse for you: do not ask that others know; do not hope for heaven’s response; constantly unify your mind — it must be firm and upright.”
[Careful in the Way] In all matters one must carefully and cautiously act according to the Way, and not turn away from it.

[Addressing Zha Dingmin, he said: “You are not yet twenty, and already you know to seek the Way; this shows a former condition. Now I name you ‘Min’; the character ‘Min’ has four meanings: keen, diligent, subtle, and quick. Keenness to dispel your darkness, diligence to spur your sloth, subtlety to open your wisdom, quickness
(swiftness)
to stir your neglect
(idleness)

. You should bethink yourself of the meaning when you hear the name, and do not think the Bodhisattva gave you a word for nothing. Further, I give you a verse: you are young indeed; you should learn filial piety and fraternal respect, and with these hold your body upright — do not be slack in your resolve.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Zha Dingmin, saying: “You have not yet reached twenty, and already you know to seek the Way; one can see that this is a former condition. Now I name you ‘Min’; the character ‘Min’ has four meanings: keen, diligent, subtle, and quick. Keenness dispels your darkness; diligence spurs your sloth; subtlety opens your wisdom; quickness guards against your idleness. You should bethink yourself of the meaning when you hear the name, and do not think the Bodhisattva gave you a single word for nothing. Further, I give you a verse: you are young indeed; you should learn filial piety and fraternal respect, and with these hold your body upright — do not slacken your resolve.”

[Not yet twenty] The age before twenty. “Weak crown”: in ancient times a male assumed the cap at twenty; because he had not yet reached strength of years, it was called the weak crown. [Filial and fraternal] Written also “xiaoti” (
tì
): being filial to parents and respectful to elder brothers.

[That day, Chen Daxin arrived late. The Bodhisattva asked him: “How do you cultivate?” He replied: “Only the Pure Land.” The Bodhisattva said: “Apart from this there is no other excellent gate. I enjoin you a verse: The Way has no other saying — only the mind; when the lotus embryo first forms, be single and undivided.”]

That day, Chen Daxin arrived only later. The Bodhisattva asked him: “How do you cultivate?” Chen Daxin answered: “I cultivate only the Pure Land.” The Bodhisattva said: “Apart from this there is no better gate. I enjoin you a verse: The Way has no other saying — only the mind; when the lotus embryo first forms, be single and undivided.”

blocks.text: The Bodhisattva’s Attainment of the Way

inline.s: [The Bodhisattva said: “The gate of the Pure Land that I have shown is truly the mind-ancestry of all Buddhas, the direct path of the human and heavenly realms
(the short road by which the human and heavenly realms escape birth and death)

. Now, though you seek rebirth, if your vow is not resolute, it is like entering the sea and not obtaining the pearl — wasted toil with no benefit. Formerly, in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Jin, I received the body of a poor child. Because of poverty I made a great vow, saying: ‘Because of
(owing to)
former karma
(the karmic offenses of former lives)

, I receive this bitter retribution. If today I do not see Amitābha Buddha and am not born in the Land of Bliss, and do not accomplish all merit, even though I lose this body, I will never retreat nor rest.’ Having made this vow, for seven days and seven nights I single-mindedly recollected, and then my mind opened, and I saw the noble marks and light of Amitābha Buddha, pervading the ten directions. Before the Buddha I personally received the prophecy, and later, at seventy-five, I sat and passed away, and was born in the Land of Bliss.]

The Bodhisattva instructed: “The Pure Land gate I have shown is truly the mind-ancestry of all Buddhas, the direct path by which the human and heavenly realms escape birth and death. Now, though you recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss, if your vow is not genuine, it is like entering the sea and not obtaining the pearl — toilsome and of no benefit. In former times, in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Jin (

), I was born as a poor man. Because of poverty, I then made a great vow: ‘Owing to the karmic offenses of my former lives, I receive this bitter retribution. If today I do not see Amitābha Buddha and am not born in the Land of Bliss, and do not accomplish all merit, even though I lose my life, I will never retreat, never rest.’ Having made the vow, for seven days and seven nights I single-mindedly recollected, and then my mind opened, and I saw the noble marks and light of Amitābha Buddha, pervading the ten directions. Before the Buddha I personally received the prophecy, and later, at seventy-five, I sat and passed away, straight to rebirth in the Western Land of Bliss. (From this one knows the Bodhisattva attained the Way in the reign of Emperor Ming of the Jin; his appearances thereafter are all manifestations.)

[Afterward, because his vow to save beings was heavy, he came again to this land, manifesting transformation in accord with each place. Sometimes a bhikshu, sometimes a layman, sometimes a king, sometimes a minister, sometimes a woman, sometimes a butcher or beggar; sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest; sometimes compliant, sometimes adverse — always he taught the Dharma in accordance with beings, guiding all the various kinds. And because those who cultivate the immortal way mostly have not awakened to the true eternal, but are sunk in the bliss of long life and do not think of further progress, I manifested an immortal body to save them from their delusion and fall — as in the affair of the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang. Now again I have set right and wrong before you and proclaimed the Pure Land. You should be of one will and one mind, and firmly cultivate this gate; you will not be misled. If your resolve is once made firm, you need not wait for rebirth in another life to see the Buddha; even now you can see the Buddha, just as I did in former years. I have a verse of four lines: speak one sentence less; recite one thought more of the Buddha’s name; beat the thought to death, and you will be allowed your Dharmakaya to live.”]

Afterward, because his vow to save beings was heavy, he came again to this land, manifesting transformation in accord with each place. Sometimes a bhikshu, sometimes a layman, sometimes a king, sometimes a minister, sometimes a woman, sometimes a butcher or beggar; sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest; sometimes compliant, sometimes adverse — always he taught the Dharma in accordance with beings, guiding and transforming beings of every faculty. And because those who cultivate the immortal way mostly have not awakened to the true eternal, but are sunk in the bliss of long life and do not think of further progress, so I manifested an immortal body to save them from the path of delusion — as in the affair of the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang (as said earlier, the Bodhisattva “in the reign of Emperor Xizong of the Tang was the eldest son of Prince Xian of Qinghe, and likewise abandoned rank to leave home”). Now again I have set right and wrong clearly before you and proclaimed the Pure Land gate. You should be of one will and one mind, and firmly cultivate this gate; you will not be misled. If your resolve is once made firm, you need not wait for life’s end and rebirth in the Land of Bliss to see Amitābha Buddha; even now you can see Amitābha Buddha, just as I did in former years. I have a verse of four lines: speak one sentence less; recite one thought more of the Buddha’s name; beat the thought to death, and you will be allowed your Dharmakaya to live.”
[Someone asked
(a person asked)

: “How can a practitioner be free of dusty desire and be without hindrance?” The Bodhisattva said: “I shall proceed from the small to the great, and from the outer to the inner; you should well understand the meaning. Suppose someone here, without reason, takes a coin from you — does anger arise?” He answered: “Though a coin is slight, being taken without reason, one is angry.” “Again, if someone gives you a coin without reason, does joy arise?” He said: “Though a coin is slight, being given without reason, one is glad.” One answered: “Since a coin is very slight, what joy is there in being given it? And nothing to be angered at in being taken.”]

A person asked: “How can a practitioner be far from dusty desire and without hindrance?” The Bodhisattva said: “I shall proceed from the small to the great, and from the outer to the inner; you must well understand its meaning. Suppose here someone takes a coin from you without reason — are you angered?” He answered: “Though a coin is small, being taken without reason, of course one is resentful.” The Bodhisattva asked: “Then, if someone gives you a coin without reason, are you pleased?” He answered: “Though a coin is small, being given without reason, of course one is delighted.” One person answered: “A coin is very small; what delight in being given it? And nothing to resent in being taken.”

[The Bodhisattva said: “If you could do this, your mind would long since have been pure; how could you, up to this day, still be sunk in defilement? You should know that practitioners wash their minds not carefully; seeing existence and non-existence, they cling everywhere, and thought after thought is greed, so that karmic consciousness stirs and scatters without a moment’s stop. Even when one recites the name Amitābha Buddha, the mind still wanders abroad, unable for an instant to return to one. This is entirely because, over immeasurable kalpas, you have never for one hour or one day roused the mind to be far from dusty desire; and so this dusty desire, from beginningless kalpas, has never for one hour or one day been willing to leave your minds. Body entwined and mind bound, you sink deep into the net of the dust — how could you be like the lotus emerging from the mud unstained?]

The Bodhisattva said: “If you were already able to do this, your mind would have been pure long ago; why to this day are you still sunk in the muddy defilement? You should know that practitioners wash the mind not finely: seeing existence and non-existence, they are stained everywhere, thought after thought is greed and anger, so that karmic consciousness stirs and scatters without a moment’s pause. Even while reciting the name Amitābha Buddha, the mind still wanders abroad, unable for an instant to return to one. This is all because, over immeasurable kalpas, you have never for one hour or one day roused a mind to be far from dusty desire; and therefore this dusty desire, from beginningless kalpas, has never for one hour or one day been willing to leave your minds. Body entwined and mind bound, you sink deep into the net of the dust — how could you be like the lotus that emerges from the mud unstained?”

[Therefore know that, to cut off greed and clinging, one should first take up the giving and taking of a single coin and practice the contemplation of renunciation, the contemplation that it is not mine. In being taken, no anger rises; in being given, no joy rises. Thus, even to hundreds and thousands of coins, even to billions and trillions of coins, even to cities, kingdoms, wives, and children, even to one’s own flesh, blood, and marrow, even to the mind, will, and consciousness of past, present, and future, even to birth and death, karmic retribution, bodhi, and nirvāṇa — all are no different from the giving and taking of this single coin. Naturally habitual leaks will die away, obstructing conditions be forever extinguished, and one will gradually tread the pure path and accomplish the factors of the Way. You should cultivate according to this; deceive no more and obstruct
(self-deception)
one another and your own
zhì ài
, hindrance and obstruction)

Therefore one knows that, to cut off greed, anger, and clinging, one should first take the giving and taking of a single coin and practice the contemplation of renunciation, the contemplation that it is not mine. In being taken, no anger rises; in being given, no joy rises. Thus, even to hundreds and thousands of coins, even to billions and trillions, even to cities, kingdoms, wives, and children, even to one’s own flesh, blood, and marrow, even to the mind, will, and consciousness of past, present, and future, even to birth and death, karmic retribution, bodhi, and nirvāṇa — all are no different from the giving and taking of this single coin. Naturally habitual tendencies and afflictions die away, obstructing conditions are forever extinguished, and one gradually becomes pure, accomplishing the factors of the Way. You should cultivate according to this, and no longer deceive and obstruct yourselves.”

[Mind, will, and consciousness] Mind has the meaning of gathering and accumulating, and is the eighth consciousness (alaya-vijnana); will has the meaning of deliberation, and is the seventh consciousness (manas-vijnana); consciousness has the meaning of discernment, and is the sixth consciousness. [Leak] A name for affliction, with the two meanings of leaking out and falling away. Greed, anger, and similar afflictions, day and night, flow out ceaselessly from the gates of the six faculties, hence they are called leaks. Moreover, affliction can make a person fall into the three evil realms, hence it is also called a leak.

blocks.text: Setting Offerings and Wishing Long Life

inline.s: [On the second day of early winter
(the first month of winter, the tenth lunar month)
, being the anniversary of the Bodhisattva’s birth, the assembly set out offerings and wished him long life. The Bodhisattva said: “With what do you honor me
(with what do you offer me birthday felicitations)

?” All said: “With the mind as offering.” The Bodhisattva said: “What thing is the mind, that it can be offered?” They replied: “Only the utmost sincerity, which in itself is nothing.” The Bodhisattva said: “Since you say it is nothing, who knows the sincerity? The one who can know the sincerity must have a place, from which it can be shown and pointed out — how can it be ‘nothing’?” They replied: “In truth, there is nothing attained.” The Bodhisattva said: “You say there is no attainment — is this a temporary absence, or a definite absence?” The assembly deliberated and could not answer.]

On the second day of the tenth month, the anniversary of the Bodhisattva’s birth, the assembly set out offerings and wished him long life. The Bodhisattva said: “With what do you offer me birthday felicitations?” All answered: “With the mind as offering.” The Bodhisattva said: “What thing is the mind, such that it can be brought as an offering?” The assembly replied: “Only the utmost sincerity, which in itself is nothing.” The Bodhisattva said: “Since you say it is nothing, who knows it to be sincere? The one who can know the sincerity must have a place, from which it can be discussed and shown — why do you say ‘nothing’?” The assembly replied: “In truth there is nothing attained.” The Bodhisattva said: “You say there is no attainment — is this a temporary absence, or a definite absence?” The assembly deliberated and gave no answer.
[With the mind as offering] To take the mind as offering; the word order is inverted for emphasis.

[The Bodhisattva said: “If it is nothing, then it is definitively nothing; if it is something, then it is definitively something. Once a hair’s doubt intervenes, a hair’s breadth becomes a thousand miles. You should know that when you speak of sincerity or falsity, of existence or non-existence, all these are minds of arising and ceasing, calculation, inference, and speculation. Offering these to me brings no benefit at all. Hear my wonderful verse: The ultimate truth has no dual mind; the ultimate truth has a measureless mind; the mind is not all minds; all natures are not mind. Apart from deluded thought, the mind is not real; relying on the true mind, a name is forced. Neither the true nor the false stand, homage to Śākyamuni the Honored One. Understand that mind has no place; expediently, bring blessings to the multitude of beings.”]

The Bodhisattva said: "If it is nothing, then it is decisively nothing; if it is something, then it is decisively something. Should there be the least doubt, then an error of a hair's breadth leads a thousand miles astray. You should know that whether you speak of sincerity or of falsity, whether you say there is a Way or say there is none, all of it is the mind of birth and death, of reckoning, of weighing and surmising. To offer me birthday wishes with such a mind brings benefit neither to you nor to me. Hear my wondrous verse: The utmost truth is the mind without duality; the utmost truth is the mind without measure. The mind is not any of the minds; no nature of anything is the mind. Doing away with the false mind, which is unreal, one leans upon the true mind, a name imposed by force. True and false alike are not established: homage to the Honored One, Śākyamuni. When the mind is understood, it has no dwelling place; by skillful means, blessing the multitude."
[Thereupon all the disciples
(the whole assembly)

bowed again and again, wishing to hear more of the essentials of the Dharma. The Bodhisattva said: "Excellent! Excellent! Since you wish to hear more of the essentials of the Dharma, you should sincerely understand my words and answer my questions well. Disciples, suppose someone said to a man: 'Yanjing is the capital where the emperor dwells; its wealth and honor are beyond compare.' Hearing this, would the man wish to go there?" All replied: "We would wish to go." The Bodhisattva said: "But if you did not know the road, what then?" All replied: "Someone would point out the way, and we would follow it." The Bodhisattva said: "That will not do. If that person pointed him southward or eastward, and he did not discern clearly but simply followed his words, then Yanjing would be farther and farther away." The assembly said: "Then what should be done?" The Bodhisattva said: "One must find someone who has actually walked to Yanjing, and have him teach this man, saying: 'You must go north, and you will go straight to the emperor's dwelling.' Disciples, was there any error in what this man pointed out?" All bowed their heads to the ground and said: "No error."]

Thereupon all the disciples bowed again and again, wishing to hear more of the essentials of the Dharma. The Bodhisattva said: "Excellent! Excellent! If you wish to hear more of the essentials of the Dharma, you should sincerely understand my words and answer my questions well. Disciples, suppose someone said to a man: 'Yanjing (present-day Beijing, so named because it was the capital of the state of Yan in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods) is the emperor's capital, its wealth and honor beyond compare.' Hearing this, would the man wish to go there?" The whole assembly answered: "We would wish to go." The Bodhisattva said: "But if you did not know the road, what then?" The whole assembly answered: "Someone would point out the way, and we would follow it." The Bodhisattva said: "That will not do. If that person pointed him southward or eastward, and he did not discern clearly but walked on according to his words, then the farther he went, the farther he would be from Yanjing." The assembly said: "Then what should be done?" The Bodhisattva said: "You must find someone who has been to Yanjing, and have him teach this man, saying: 'You must walk north, and you will go straight to Yanjing.' Disciples, was there any error in what this man pointed out?" The whole assembly bowed and said: "No error."

[The Bodhisattva said: "Again, suppose a man wished to climb a peak ten thousand fathoms high, the top of a nine-storied tower, how should he be taught?" All said: "From the low to the high." The Bodhisattva said: "So it is. The ancients said: 'A journey of a thousand miles begins beneath one's feet.' It must be from the first step to the second, and so on up to the highest, and only that is right teaching. To say that one leap carries you to the very top is wild talk
(random nonsense)

. Again, suppose the emperor were about to appoint a man to office, and sent him a decree: 'Would you rather be prime minister, or a petty clerk?' How should the man reply?" All said: "He would surely wish to be prime minister." The Bodhisattva said: "So it is. Again, suppose a man stood at a forked road, not knowing which way to take. Someone who pitied him pointed and said: 'This way is exceedingly hard and dangerous, exceedingly crooked; you will never get through
(you will never get out)

. That way is exceedingly broad and straight, exceedingly level; walk it and you will get through.' Receiving this direction, which of the two roads should the man take?" All said: "The broad one, the level one." The Bodhisattva said: "Excellent! Excellent! Your answers to my questions all accord with right principle. But can you clearly understand my parables?" All bowed again and said: "We only pray you to disclose the teaching."]

The Bodhisattva said: "Again, suppose a man wished to climb a mountain peak ten thousand fathoms high, the top of a nine-storied tower, how should he be taught?" The whole assembly answered: "From the low to the high." The Bodhisattva said: "So it is. The ancients said: 'A journey of a thousand miles begins beneath one's feet.' It must be from the first step to the second, and so on up to the highest; that alone is right teaching. To say that one step leaps to the very top is random nonsense. Again, suppose the emperor were about to give a man office, and sent a decree asking him: 'Would you rather be prime minister, or a petty clerk?' How would this man answer?" The whole assembly answered: "He would certainly wish to be prime minister." The Bodhisattva said: "So it is. Again, suppose a man stood at a forked road, not knowing which way to take. Someone who pitied him pointed and said: 'This road is exceedingly hard and dangerous, exceedingly crooked, you will never get out. That road is exceedingly broad and straight, exceedingly level; walk it and you will get out.' Receiving his direction, which road should the man take?" The whole assembly answered: "The broad one, the level one." The Bodhisattva said: "Excellent! Excellent! Your answers to my questions all accord with right principle. But can you clearly understand my parables?" The whole assembly bowed again and said: "We only pray the Bodhisattva to disclose the teaching."

[The Bodhisattva said: "Listen well. Hitherto, though you have had the mind that seeks the Way, you have not understood the essentials of practice; your direction has had no ground, like a man who wishes to go to Yanjing but does not know the road. If he meets a false teacher who teaches him a false dharma, it is as though the imperial capital lay to the north and he were pointed east or south instead. Then though that man walks all day long, he wanders with no place to return to; how could he ever have audience
jìn
, to have audience with a sovereign or pay homage at a holy place)

with the Most Honored One? How could he ever accomplish the great Way? The Pure Land of Amitābha that I now point out is the imperial capital. Faith, vow, and practice, the three, diligently and with ever greater effort, at last attaining rebirth: this is to go from the first step to the highest. To aspire to the upper grades is to wish to be prime minister, not to be a petty clerk. To cultivate in accord with this is to walk the broad and straight road and not the crooked one. I am one who has walked to Yanjing. If you cannot deeply believe, then you are abandoning the imperial capital to rush to the frontier, casting aside the eminence of prime minister to take up the meanness of a petty clerk, turning your back on the broad and straight to seek the hard and narrow. The peak ten thousand fathoms high and the top of the nine-storied tower will be beyond your reach; how deeply pitiable!"]

The Bodhisattva said: "Now gather your minds and listen attentively. Hitherto, though you have had the mind that seeks the Way, you have not understood the essential path of practice, nor how you ought to cultivate, and you have had no right ground to rely on. This is like a man who wishes to go to Yanjing but does not know the road. If he meets a false teacher who teaches him a false dharma, it is as though Yanjing lay to the north and he were instead pointed east or south. Then though this man cultivates diligently all day long, he wanders with no place to return to; how could he ever have audience (
jìn

, to have audience with a sovereign or pay homage at a holy place) with the Most Honored One? How could he ever accomplish the great Way? The Pure Land of Amitābha that I now disclose is the imperial capital. With faith, vow, and practice all complete, diligently and with ever greater effort, at last attaining rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, this is to go from the first step to the highest. To aspire to the upper grades is to wish to be prime minister, not to be a petty clerk. To cultivate in accord with this is to walk the broad and straight road and not the crooked one. I am one who has been to Yanjing. If you cannot deeply believe, then you are abandoning the imperial capital to rush to the frontier, casting aside the eminence of prime minister to take up the meanness of a petty clerk, turning your back on the broad and straight to seek the hard and narrow. Then the peak ten thousand fathoms high and the top of the nine-storied tower will be beyond your reach; truly pitiable and grievous!"
[The assembly wished to acquire fields as a provision for practice. The Bodhisattva said: "You wish to pledge your resolve to study together
(you vow to cultivate and study together)

, to gather for long and never scatter, to renounce worldly affairs, and no longer to seek from others for the source of clothing and food, and so you have raised this proposal. As I see it, though the thought is good, it is after all a craving for the toil of the dust, not a pure dharma. Why is that? A meal at the street corner and a night's rest among the graves
zhǒng
, grave)

, such was the model of the former Buddhas' practice of the Way. If you must rely on fields in order to practice, then should the fields not be obtained, you and all these people would never have a day for practice."]

The assembly wished to buy fields as a source of clothing and food for practice. The Bodhisattva said: "You vow to study together, to gather for long and never scatter, to renounce worldly affairs, and no longer to seek from others for the source of clothing and food; that is why you have held this discussion. As I see it, though the thought is good, it is after all a craving for the toil of the dust, not a pure dharma. Why is that? A meal at the street corner and a night's rest among the graves, this is the model of the former Buddhas' cultivation of the Way. If one must rely on fields as a source of livelihood in order to practice, then if the fields cannot be obtained, none of you will ever have a day of practice.
[Again, if you say that you have no funds
(the same as 'resources')
of your own and will go out to solicit donations, that is even less permissible. In the Buddha's teaching of one whole age there are no such two words
(no such words as 'soliciting donations')

. It is the doing of people of the final age who do not know propriety and righteousness, do not fear cause and effect, and know no shame. A true cultivator of the Way keeps the thought of birth and death close at heart and would never entertain such a notion. Yet I have one more word: if you all simply hold fast to right mindfulness and each strive on your own, then you are gathered though not gathered. If body and mind are slack and scattered, and your affairs have no constancy, then you are scattered though gathered. If you understand this meaning, you should simply follow your portion and the time, and not go in for idle thoughts and calculations."]

Moreover, if you had no such funds of your own and must go out to solicit donations, that is even less permissible. In the Buddha's teaching of one whole age there are no such words as 'soliciting donations.' All of that is the doing of people of the final age who do not know propriety and righteousness, do not fear cause and effect, and know no shame. A true cultivator of the Way keeps the thought of birth and death close at heart and would never have such a thought. Yet I have more to enjoin upon you: if you all simply hold fast to right mindfulness and each strive on your own, then that is to be gathered without gathering. If body and mind are slack and scattered and you cannot keep to it constantly, then that is to be scattered though gathered. If you understand this principle, you should simply follow your portion and the time, and not go in for idle thoughts and calculations."
[The teaching of one whole age] That is, the teaching of one whole age, what Śākyamuni Buddha

set forth during the whole span of his life from the attainment of the Way to his entry into nirvāṇa: the three baskets, the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the eighty-four thousand dharma doors, and so on.

[The Bodhisattva again told the assembly: "Are you troubled that your bodies are entangled in the net of the world, so that your thoughts cannot be clean? I have a method. You need only arouse the vow to leave and seek deliverance, take the mind that firmly turns toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss and beholds Amitābha Buddha,
and exchange it for
the mind that rushes to and fro after profit and fame, and you will then be able to walk the road of awakening even amid the toil of the dust."]

The Bodhisattva again said to the assembly: "Are you troubled that your bodies are entangled in the net of the world, so that your thoughts cannot be clean? I have a method. You need only arouse the vow to leave the Saha world and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, and take the mind that firmly turns toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss and beholds Amitābha Buddha, exchanging it for the mind that rushes about after profit and fame; then you will be able to walk the road of awakening amid the toil of the dust."

[Someone asked: "When reciting the Buddha's name one cannot attain single-mindedness; what skillful means should one use?" The Bodhisattva said: "You need only still your thoughts and settle your mind, and recite gently on, causing the sound to accord with the mind and the mind to follow the sound. Recite long, and of itself all thoughts will clear, mind and object will both be cut off from illumination, and you will enter the Buddha-recitation samadhi. Yet in ordinary times you must recite much, from a thousand to ten thousand, with no break in the mind; then the faculties ripen most easily. If you force it into oneness, in the end it will not be one." At that time, Daben, seated below, suddenly woke with a start
jué
and recited several times. The Bodhisattva said: "Thus it is. Thus it is."]

Someone asked: "When reciting the Buddha's name one cannot attain single-mindedness; what skillful means should one use?" The Bodhisattva said: "You need only still your thoughts and settle your mind, and recite gently on, causing the sound to accord with the mind and the mind to follow the sound. Recite long, and of itself all thoughts will clear; mind and object will both be cut off, and you will enter the Buddha-recitation samadhi. Yet in ordinary times you must recite much, from a thousand to ten thousand, with no break in the mind, and then the faculties ripen most easily. If you force it into oneness, in the end it will not be one." At this time Daben, seated below, suddenly woke with a start and recited the Buddha's name several times. The Bodhisattva said: "Thus it is. Thus it is."

[The disciples wished to fashion an image and make offerings, and asked the Bodhisattva to indicate the marks of the dharma-form. The Bodhisattva said: "You disciples wish to fashion an image and make offerings, and have long accumulated sincerity; it should indeed be shown. But you are amid the toil of the dust
(but you are amid the toil of the dust)
and I am within wonderful clarity
(while I am within wonderful clarity)

, so even were it shown now, you could not see it. Moreover, I transform beings according to their capacities, and my bodily marks are not one. For now, simply take my form as it was when I first began to cultivate
(now take the form in which I first began to cultivate)
, and you may paint it as the form of a great bhikshu: face like the full moon, body full and stalwart
(full and stalwart of form)

, wearing the kashaya and seated upon a lotus, left hand resting on the knee, right hand in the mudra of expounding the Dharma, a white-curl light streaming from between the eyebrows, and within that light Amitābha Buddha seated in full lotus. You must
(you must)
make the marks majestic and fine, and not be slipshod." When the people heard this, they all stood with hands folded
(standing respectfully at attention)

and contemplated this dharma-form. The Bodhisattva then said: "Disciples, each person has a Jue Ming Miao Xing [bodhisattva], neither identical with him nor apart from him, appearing at every moment where you cannot grope for it. Now that you understand, there is no further need to set up an image and make offerings; I hope to see you another day."]

The disciples prepared to fashion an image and make offerings to the Bodhisattva, and asked him to indicate the marks of the dharma-form. The Bodhisattva said: "You disciples wish to fashion an image and make offerings, and have reverently planned it for a long time; it should indeed be shown. But you are amid the toil of the dust, while I am within wonderful clarity; even were it shown, you could not see it. Moreover, I transform beings according to their capacities, and my bodily marks are not one. For now, take the form in which I first began to cultivate: you may paint it as the form of a great bhikshu, face like the full moon, body full and stalwart, wearing the kashaya and seated upon a lotus, left hand resting on the knee, right hand in the mudra of expounding the Dharma, a white-curl light streaming from between the eyebrows, and within that light Amitābha Buddha seated in full lotus. You must make the marks majestic and fine, and not be slipshod." When the people had heard this, they all stood respectfully and contemplated this dharma-form. The Bodhisattva then said: "Disciples, each person has a Jue Ming Miao Xing [bodhisattva], neither identical with him nor apart from him, appearing at every moment where you cannot grope for it. Now that you understand this, there is no further need to set up an image and make offerings; may we meet again another day."
[Face like the full moon] A face round and fair, like the full moon, describing a countenance white, pure, full, and spirited. [Cross-legged (
jiā fū

) seated] Both feet crossed and placed upon the left and right thighs is called the 'full cross-legged sitting.' Placing only the left foot over the right thigh, or only the right foot over the left thigh, is called 'half cross-legged sitting.'

blocks.text: Renouncing the Household to Become a Monk

inline.s: [Zha Dinghong, because he had lost his son, wished to renounce the household and become a monk. The Bodhisattva said: "Do not indulge in vain thoughts of this matter; this matter is not yours to do. You need only set your mind right to govern the mind, set your body right to govern the body, cut off unprofitable affairs, forsake unprofitable friends, take refuge in the Great Awakening, and vow to leave the deluded path. Draw up
yì
, to draw up)

that vast flood to nourish my parched soil; earnestly seek the added blessing, and drive away all obstructive conditions. You have always revered prayers for long life and protection of the body; you should focus your strength on this, and say no more." Dinghong then asked: "I have received the teaching to hold the Diamond Sutra, but there are various passages whose wording differs; which edition should I follow so as to be free of error?" The Bodhisattva said: "The seven words 'Vajra Prajna Paramita' are free of all error."]

Zha Dinghong, having lost his son, wished to renounce the household and become a monk. The Bodhisattva said: "Do not indulge in vain thoughts of this matter; this matter is not yours to do. You need only set your mind right to govern the mind, and set your body right to govern the body (rectify your own conduct in order to correct former crooked conduct), cut off unprofitable affairs, forsake unprofitable friends, take refuge in the Buddha, and vow to leave the deluded path. Use the Dharma to nourish your parched heart, earnestly seek the Buddha's added blessing, and drive away all obstructive conditions. You have always revered prayers for long life and protection of the body, and such prayers should focus their strength here; say no more." Zha Dinghong then asked: "I have received the teaching to hold and uphold the Diamond Sutra, but among the various editions there are passages whose wording differs; which should I follow so as to be free of error?" The Bodhisattva said: "The seven words 'Vajra Prajna Paramita' are free of all error."
[Great Awakening]
The great awakening, that is, the Buddha's awakening. Here it means the Buddha.

blocks.text: Illness and the Request for Instruction

inline.s: [Shen Tianyu was ill and made offerings to request instruction. The Bodhisattva said: "You are now ill, but not yet at the point of death. You should put to rest all your entanglements, calm your mind and sit upright, contemplate the impermanence of the body, contemplate the impermanence of the world, lay down every deluded condition, and gently recite a single phrase, Amitābha Buddha. Of itself the six dusts will not arise, and the one mind will be pure. Not only will this cure the illness of your present life; the very root of the illness of birth and death will be pulled out from this."]

Shen Tianyu was ill and made offerings to request the Bodhisattva's instruction. The Bodhisattva said: "You are now ill, but not yet at the point of death. You should put to rest all your entanglements, calm your mind and sit upright, contemplate the impermanence of the body, contemplate the impermanence of the world, lay down every deluded condition, and gently recite a single phrase, Amitābha Buddha. Of itself the six dusts will not arise, and the one mind will be pure. Not only will this cure the illness of your present life; the very root of the illness of birth and death will be pulled out from this.

[You now make offerings to request instruction, merely hoping that I have some fine prescription for you, some wondrous oral formula to transmit to you that can cure your illness. Little do you know that a bodhisattva has no such false dharmas; he simply teaches you with these few solid, true words. If you believe and put them into practice, they are truly one dose of the finest elixir and wonder-drug. I give you a verse: Illness is made by oneself, and by oneself it is removed; gather the mind to purity, and attain constant peace and joy, firm and long without change, the same as Measureless Life."]

You now make offerings to request my instruction, merely hoping that I have some good prescription for you, some wondrous oral formula to transmit to you that can cure your illness. Little do you know that a bodhisattva has no such false dharmas; he simply teaches you with these few solid, true words. If you believe and put them into practice, they are truly one dose of the finest golden elixir and wonder-drug. I give you a verse: Illness is made by oneself, and by oneself it is removed; gather the mind to purity, and attain constant peace and joy, firm and long without change, the same as Measureless Life."
[Reverted Elixir] Also called the golden elixir,
an immortal pill made by the Daoists through refining the nine-times-cycled elixir together with cinnabar; it is said that one who takes it can become an immortal at once.
[The Bodhisattva instructed Daben, saying: "You wish to investigate and clarify the mind-ground, a most worthy resolve. But your belly is stuffed with sand, lead, water, and fire
(the arts of alchemy)

, so that such words as 'original face' and 'true emptiness, true purity' are utterly blocked up; how can you do it? If you wish to do it, you must fling this whole tangle into the Eastern Ocean before you can. Otherwise you will waste your mind and ruin your effort. Better to recite one phrase, Amitābha Buddha, solidly and truly: clarifying the mind lies here, and rebirth in the Pure Land lies here, one act and two gains, an excellent bargain."]

The Bodhisattva instructed Daben, saying: "You wish to investigate and clarify the mind-ground, a most worthy resolve. But your belly is stuffed with the arts of alchemy, so that such principles as 'original face' and 'true emptiness, true purity' are utterly blocked up by this rubbish; how can you do it? If you wish to investigate and clarify the mind-ground, you must fling this whole tangle into the Eastern Ocean before you can. Otherwise you will waste your mind and ruin your effort. Better to recite one phrase, Amitābha Buddha, solidly and truly: clarifying the mind lies here, and rebirth in the Pure Land lies here, one act and two gains, an excellent bargain!"

[Clarifying the mind lies here, rebirth in the Pure Land lies here, one act and two gains] When Buddha-recitation reaches single-mindedness without confusion, one is at once reborn in the Pure Land; when one enters the Buddha-recitation samadhi, one at once clarifies the mind-ground.
[Wuxiu asked: "How may one repay grandfather and father
(grandfather and father)

?" The Bodhisattva said: "Among the filial acts spoken of in the world, which is the highest?" He said: "To be able to support them respectfully, to be able to do good, and not to forget the virtue of one's forebears." The Bodhisattva said: "This is indeed filial, yet it is limited. Only one who can arouse great vows and cultivate the dharma of world-transcendence: if the Way is accomplished and the fruit fulfilled, not only will blessing reach nine generations of ancestors; even enemies and kin throughout the kalpas will all receive liberation. If you can devote yourself to the Pure Land, that is great filial piety."]

Wuxiu asked: "How may I repay the deep kindness of my grandfather and father?" The Bodhisattva said: "Among filial acts spoken of in the world, which is best?" Wuxiu replied: "To be able to support them respectfully, to be able to do good, and not to forget the virtue of one's forebears." The Bodhisattva said: "This is indeed filial, yet after all it is limited. Only one who can arouse great vows and cultivate the dharma of world-transcendence: if the Way is accomplished and the fruit fulfilled, not only will blessing reach nine generations of ancestors (a general term for all ancestors of past generations); even enemies and kin throughout the kalpas will all receive liberation. If you can devote yourself exclusively to the Pure Land dharma door, that is great filial piety."

blocks.text: Holding the Mantra, Clarifying the Mind

inline.s: [Dingmao asked: "How does holding the mantra clarify the mind? What is the ultimate?" The Bodhisattva said: "The mind does not leave the mantra, the mantra does not leave the mind; that is the meaning of holding. At all times you should contemplate this mantra-essence: is it one with my mind-essence, or two? If you say two, how can the mind hold the mantra and the mantra reveal the mind? If you say one, how is it that when you forget, the mantra is not, and when you remember, the mantra is? Then you know that this mantra and the mind are apart from all names and marks, and are ultimately empty and still; this is called the ultimate. If you merely hold without the ultimate, then there is no wondrous understanding; how can the great wisdom of equality manifest? If the great wisdom of equality does not appear, how can it illumine the stupor of birth and death and reach the reality of the three realms?"]

Dingmao asked: "How does holding the mantra clarify the mind? What is the ultimate?" The Bodhisattva said: "The mind does not leave the mantra one holds, and the mantra one holds does not leave the mind; this is the meaning of holding the mantra. (The above answers 'how does holding the mantra clarify the mind.') At all times you must contemplate this mantra-essence: is it one with my mind-essence, or two? If you say two, why can the mind hold the mantra and the mantra reveal the mind? If you say one, why is it that when you forget to hold it there is no mantra, and when you remember to hold it there is a mantra? Then you know that this mantra and the mind are apart from all names and marks, and are ultimately empty and still; this is called the ultimate. (The above answers 'what is the ultimate.') If you merely hold without the ultimate, then there is no wondrous understanding; how can the great wisdom of equality manifest? If the great wisdom of equality does not appear, how can it illumine the stupor of birth and death and reach the reality of the three realms?"

[Daben asked: "When reciting the Buddha's name aloud, one easily rises in fire; may one recite silently?" The Bodhisattva said: "The moment you recite the Buddha's name you say fire arises; why is it that when you talk to people all day long, not the least fire arises? You should know that this fire is the accumulation of your ignorance and afflictions throughout measureless kalpas; because your faith today is not true, the recitation follows the fire, and the fire follows delusion, burning your dharma-body and wisdom-life. Formerly Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the great Dharma, throughout measureless kalpas gave up his body seeking the Way, and so attained the unsurpassed treasure king."]

Daben asked: "When reciting the Buddha's name aloud, one easily rises in fire; may one recite silently?" The Bodhisattva said: "The moment you recite the Buddha's name you speak of fire arising; why is it that when you talk aloud to people all day long, not the least fire arises? You should know that the fire you speak of is the accumulation of your ignorance and afflictions throughout measureless kalpas; because your faith now is not true and earnest, the recitation follows the fire, and the fire follows delusion, burning up your dharma-body and wisdom-life. Formerly Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the great Dharma, throughout measureless kalpas gave up his body seeking the Way, and so attained the unsurpassed treasure king.

The Bodhisattva not only revealed the reason why Daben rose in fire when reciting the Buddha's name, but also, taking the World-Honored One's giving up of his body seeking the Way throughout measureless kalpas as an example, reproved Daben for his retreat.

[You are now old and your strength failing; even cultivating day and night you would still think it too late, yet you still cling to the toil of the dust, hoping for elixirs to prolong your years. Have you not heard that even the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception still has an end to its reward, and that the fire of the kalpa burns through, destroying as far as the third dhyana heaven? How much less can the petty compounding of water, fire, lead, and mercury, a dharma of borrowed causes and conditions, be sought for permanence without change? Now that you hear my words, you should be like one waking from a dream, like one sobering from drink: cultivate the Pure Land with precision, and be reborn with right mindfulness. The lifespan of that world is without end; you will accomplish the dharma-body and reach omniscience. This cannot be spoken of in the same day as the shallow art of long life and enduring sight."]

You are now old and your strength failing; even cultivating day and night you would still think it too late, and yet you still cling to the dusty world, hoping to refine elixirs to prolong your years. Have you not heard that even the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception still has a time when its lifespan ends, when the fire of the kalpa burns through and destroys as far as the third dhyana heaven? How much less can one hope for permanence of life by taking the petty elixirs compounded of water, fire, lead, and mercury, dharmas of borrowed causes and conditions? Now that you hear my words, you should be like one waking from a dream, like one sobering from drink: cultivate the Pure Land with precision and be reborn with right mindfulness. The lifespan of that world is without end, and one accomplishes the dharma-body and reaches omniscience; this far cannot be mentioned in the same breath as the shallow art of long life and enduring sight."
[The Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception]
Abbreviated from the Heaven of Neither Thought nor No-Thought, the summit of the three realms, with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas.

[The four kalpas] Within one great kalpa there are four intermediate kalpas: the kalpa of formation, the kalpa of duration, the kalpa of destruction, and the kalpa of emptiness; and each intermediate kalpa in turn has twenty small kalpas. 'Formation' means that the world is assembled from the convergence of many conditions; 'duration' means that living beings dwell there, with plants and animals, with lands and histories; 'destruction' means the beginning of ruin: in the first nineteen small kalpas all plants and animals are destroyed, and in the last small kalpa the land-world on which beings rely is destroyed; 'emptiness' means that after all is destroyed, everything becomes empty space. Thus the world endlessly forms, endures, is destroyed, and becomes empty, over and over again. [The fire of the kalpa burns through, destroying as far as the third dhyana heaven] The great fire of the kalpa of destruction blazes, burning from the hells up to the third dhyana heaven of the form realm, and the world is reduced to ashes. [The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of lust and food, and includes the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the realm of form is the world inhabited by beings who are free of the two desires of lust and food but still have a physical body, and includes the four dhyana heavens and the eighteen heavens; the formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who have no physical body but dwell with their consciousness in profound and wondrous samadhi, and includes the four formless heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all the territory of the birth-and-death round of ordinary beings. [The eighteen heavens] The eighteen heavens of the realm of form: the first dhyana heaven has three heavens, namely the Heaven of Brahma's Multitude, the Heaven of Brahma's Ministers, and the Great Brahma Heaven; the second dhyana heaven also has three, namely the Heaven of Lesser Light, the Heaven of Measureless Light, and the Heaven of Light-Sound; the third dhyana heaven also has three, namely the Heaven of Lesser Purity, the Heaven of Measureless Purity, and the Heaven of Universal Purity; the fourth dhyana heaven has nine in all, namely the Heaven Without Clouds, the Heaven of Blessing-Birth, the Heaven of Vast Fruit, the Heaven Without Thought, the Heaven Without Affliction, the Heaven Without Heat, the Heaven of Good Seeing, the Heaven of Good Manifestation, and the Heaven of the Utmost of Form. [Enduring sight] The functions of ear and eye not declining.

[Zha Dinghong asked: "When holding the mantra, much terror arises; I beg you to show me a skillful means." The Bodhisattva said: "Who is it that terrifies you? Who is it that is terrified? Because the habitual tendencies of your former lives are impure, this appearance suddenly manifests from subtle thought. You need only recite and hold it earnestly and sincerely, and of itself it will be removed; you will gain compliance of mind and will, be well able to subdue afflictions, and enter into the profound and subtle. What terror is there?"]

Zha Dinghong asked: "When holding the mantra, much terror arises; I beg the Bodhisattva to show me a method." The Bodhisattva said: "Who terrifies you? Who is the one terrified? Because the habitual tendencies of your former lives are impure, this appearance of terror suddenly manifests from subtle thought (subtle thought-moments); that is all. You need only recite and hold it earnestly and sincerely, and the habitual tendencies will of themselves be removed; you will gain compliance of mind and will, be well able to subdue afflictions, and enter into the profound and subtle. What terror could remain?"

blocks.text: Filial Piety, First of Ten Thousand Virtues

inline.s: [Chen Dingyu prayed on behalf of his mother's illness and asked: "What merit should I make so that she may be fully healed?" The Bodhisattva showed a verse, saying: "Filial piety is first of ten thousand virtues; filial piety penetrates the Three Powers
(Heaven, Earth, and Humanity)
, great indeed is the practice of filial piety; human relations
(the relations and standards of conduct among people)

have it for their teacher. With a good heart you seek your mother's recovery; when you are at ease, remember your mother's pain; when you eat fine food, remember your mother eating less; when you wear soft garments, remember your mother's pus and blood staining her clothing, her breast and sides exposed
(from the chest to the armpits)

, think thus, and night and day have no rest. Take refuge in the Great Sage, single-minded and sincere, and earnestly practice all good, to repay the four kindnesses from above. May your mother's blessings increase, may your mother's lifespan increase, may your mother's illness be cured, may your mother's body be well. The Bodhisattva Jue Ming is your reliance
yī hù
, to rely on)
; if you act as he says, there is no vow unfulfilled."]

Chen Dingyu prayed for his mother in her illness and asked: "What merit should I make so that my mother may be healed?" The Bodhisattva showed a verse, saying: "Filial piety is first of ten thousand virtues (filial piety is the head of all virtues); filial piety penetrates the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity); great indeed is the practice of filial piety; human relations (the relations and standards of conduct among people) have it for their teacher. With a good heart you seek your mother's recovery; when you are at ease, remember your mother's pain; when you eat fine food, remember your mother eating less; when you wear soft garments, remember your mother's pus and blood staining her clothing, her breast and sides exposed (from the chest to the armpits); think thus, and night and day have no rest. Take refuge in the Great Sage, single-minded and sincere, and earnestly practice all good, to repay the four kindnesses from above. May your mother's blessings increase, may your mother's lifespan increase, may your mother's illness be cured, may your mother's body be well. The Bodhisattva Jue Ming is your reliance (
yī hù
, to rely on), if you act according to his words, no vow will fail."

The verse above means: filial piety is the first of ten thousand virtues; filial piety can move Heaven, Earth, and Humanity. The practice of filial piety is vast and great; it is the teacher of all human relations. With your fine filial heart you seek your mother's recovery. When you are at ease and comfortable, think of the pain your mother suffered in bearing you; when you eat fine food, think of how your mother went short of food and clothing to raise you; when you wear good clothes, think how at your birth the pus and blood soiled her garments and her breast and sides were left uncovered. Pondering thus, day and night you will find no rest. Only by taking refuge in the Buddha, single-minded and sincere, and striving to do every good deed, can you repay the kindness of parents, living beings, the state, and the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha). And may your mother gain blessing and years, be cured of illness, and enjoy good health. The Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing is your reliance; if you act according to the Bodhisattva's words, every wish will be fulfilled.

blocks.text: Setting Aside the Mantra to Recite the Buddha's Name

inline.s: [Dingmao wished to set aside holding the mantra and instead recite the Buddha's name, and asked about it. The Bodhisattva said: "You wish to set aside holding the mantra and recite the Buddha's name, devoting yourself single-mindedly to one practice; most excellent. But you do not yet know the essentials of the Dharma; you can only be called a person who keeps the precepts, eats vegetarian, and loves goodness; you cannot be called a person who recites the Buddha's name. Why is that? To cross the great ocean one must have a great ship; to gallop a thousand miles one must choose a good horse. Therefore one who recites the Buddha's name must first possess great means: cut off all entanglements, break open the net of dust, and directly, the very recitation is the Buddha, the very Buddha is the mind, and further, beyond both identity and difference, suddenly enter the Tathagata's treasury of great light. Only thus is it called reciting the Buddha with right mindfulness, and only thus may one be named a person who recites the Buddha's name. You should understand this meaning well."]

Dingmao wished to give up reciting the mantra and practice Buddha-recitation instead, and asked the Bodhisattva about it. The Bodhisattva said: "You wish to forsake the mantra and practice reciting the Buddha's name, single-mindedly devoted — nothing could be better. But you do not yet know the essentials of Buddha-recitation, so you can only be called a person who keeps the fasts and loves goodness, not yet a person who recites the Buddha's name. Why is this? To cross the great sea one must have a great boat; to gallop a thousand li one must choose a fine horse. Therefore a person who recites the Buddha's name must first possess great ability, cut off all entanglements, and break through the net of the world. Directly, the very recitation is the Buddha, the very Buddha is the mind — even beyond both forsaking and beyond affirming, one suddenly enters the Tathagata's great treasury of light. Only then is it called right-mindfulness Buddha-recitation, and only then may one be called a person who recites the Buddha's name. You should understand this meaning well."
[The net of the world]
People in this world are bound by all kinds of constraints, like fish in a net, hence it is called the net of the world.

Four young monks then came to call on the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva said: "O young ones, from beginningless time sentient beings have, because of love and affection, become family and kin. And among kin, parents toward their children hold the heaviest grace and the keenest love, hard to cut and hard to let go. Now you have left the world, that is, you are fully ordained as monks; you should know that toward you your parents have a grace upon grace, beyond words
(beyond what speech can express)

. Therefore you should seize the vigor of this prime of life to diligently advance on the Way, and repay your parents' whole-hearted resolve in first cutting off affection and severing love — only then will you be worthy of these two words 'left the world.' If you instead give yourselves over to indulgence and sloth, so that your whole life comes to waste and decline
(so that your whole life ruins your practice of the Way and falls back)
, then this is the unfilial among the unfilial, a most grievous sinner under heaven. Because of my words, you should be stirred to deep and urgent reflection."

Four young monks came to call on the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva said: "O young ones, from beginningless time sentient beings have, because of love and affection, become family and kin. And among kin, parents toward their children hold the heaviest grace and the keenest love, hard to cut and hard to let go. Now that you have left the world and have become monks, you should know that toward you your parents have a grace upon grace, which speech cannot express. Therefore you should seize the vigor of this prime of life to diligently advance on the Way, and repay your parents' whole-hearted resolve in first cutting off affection and severing love in sending you forth — only then will you be worthy of these two words 'left the world.' If you give yourselves over to indulgence and sloth, so that your whole life ruins your practice of the Way and falls back, then you are the unfilial among the unfilial, a most grievous sinner under heaven. Hearing these words of mine, you should be stirred to deep and urgent reflection."

The Bodhisattva again instructed the assembly, saying: "O good men, this body of a person is born of parents, nurtured by parents.
