You must understand this principle."

blocks.text: One Asks about One's Whole Life

inline.s: Someone asked about his whole life. The Bodhisattva said: "You ask about your whole life? I have here no method for determining a whole life, because the Bodhisattva, in practicing through kalpa after kalpa, never learned such a matter. Yet you are indeed too foolish: a whole life is no more than this, so what is the use of asking about it? Why do you not ask, when your head has turned white, your face has wrinkled, your body has grown weak, and impermanence is about to arrive, how you are to face King Yama with a single half-sentence, so as to avoid going off in shackles and chains? Why do you not ask about this matter?"

Someone asked about his whole life. The Bodhisattva said: "You ask about your whole life? I have no method here for determining a whole life, because the Bodhisattva, in practicing through kalpa after kalpa, never learned such fortune-telling. Yet you are indeed too foolish: a whole life is no more than this, so what is the use of asking about it? Why do you not ask, when your head has turned white, your face has wrinkled, your body has grown weak, and impermanence is about to arrive, how before King Yama you are to match him with a single half-sentence, so as to avoid going off in shackles and chains? Why do you not ask about this matter?"
[Asking about one's whole life, asking about one's final destiny]

The true answer to asking about one's whole life and asking about one's final destiny is this: though a little poorer, a little more ill, a little more frustrated, a little shorter-lived — as long as at death one is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, then the whole life is a good whole life, and that final destiny is a blissful final destiny. Conversely, though somewhat richer, healthier, smoother, longer-lived — if at death one cannot be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, then the whole life is a bad whole life, and that final destiny is a miserable final destiny. Therefore, rather than care about poverty or wealth, sickness or health, adversity or ease, an early or a late death, it is better to care about how to recite the Buddha well. And moreover, poverty or wealth, sickness or health, adversity or ease, an early or a late death are often beyond one's control, whereas whether one recites the Buddha well lies within my own grasp. So to recite the Buddha well is the wondrous method that settles everything once and for all; over the rest there is no need to be too concerned.

[The monk Fayuan was about to enter a repentance retreat before Amitābha, and first came to ask for instruction. The Bodhisattva said: “The Amitābha Repentance was compiled in recent times by the Repentance Master Ciyun, and it likewise holds the single-mindedness of phenomenon and principle
(it also possesses single-mindedness in the phenomenal and in the principled sense)
. Single-mindedness in the phenomenal sense is to focus on a single affair; if the four marks
(the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a life-span)

do not arise, and one is as clear as empty space, this is called single-mindedness in the principled sense, and this single-mindedness is hard to reach. Outwardly, diligently practice the repentance to remove past karmic obstacles; inwardly, contemplate according to principle, gradually arriving at single-mindedness. Once you attain single-mindedness, how can you worry about not entering the Way? You, now in this retreat, do not concern yourself with whether it is for yourself or for the donors, nor with how long or short it is; only sweep away your habitual tendencies, scour your body and mind, and if you do not attain samādhi, vow not to rest - that is all.]

The monk Fayuan was about to enter a repentance retreat before Amitābha, and first came to ask for instruction. The Bodhisattva said: “The Amitābha Repentance was compiled in recent times by the Repentance Master Ciyun, and it also includes single-mindedness in both the phenomenal and the principled senses. Single-mindedness in the phenomenal sense is to focus on a single affair; if the four marks (the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a life-span) do not arise, and one is as clear as empty space, this is called single-mindedness in the principled sense, and this single-mindedness free of distraction is hard to reach. Outwardly, diligently practice the repentance to remove past karmic obstacles; inwardly, contemplate according to principle, gradually arriving at single-mindedness. Once you attain single-mindedness free of distraction, how can you worry about not entering the Way? You, in this retreat, do not concern yourself with whether it is for yourself or for the donors, nor with how long or short it is; only sweep away your habitual tendencies, scour your body and mind, and if you do not attain samādhi, vow not to rest - that is all.”

[Moreover, you are there; even if you proceed in good order, it is not a place for cultivation. If you truly wish to cultivate, let go of the myriad conditions, rely with one bowl upon the ten directions, with one body upon the great earth, and, truly and earnestly, seek to be delivered from birth and death - this is the true method of cultivation. If in a paltry three-year
(three years)

repentance period, mingled with worldly affairs, one wishes to accomplish the pure karma and escape birth and death, it is like breathing the wind and swallowing the mist to seek fullness - a thing that can never be in this world. Do not harbor this great deluded thought, and end up dying of cold and hunger.”]

Moreover, you are there repenting before Amitābha; although you proceed in good order, it is not a place for cultivation. If you truly wish to cultivate, let go of the myriad conditions, rely with one bowl upon the ten directions, with one body upon the great earth, and, truly and earnestly, seek to be delivered from birth and death - this is the true method of cultivation. If in a paltry three-year repentance period, mingled with worldly affairs, one wishes to accomplish the pure karma and escape birth and death, it is like breathing the wind and swallowing the mist to seek fullness - a thing that can never be in this world. Do not harbor this great deluded thought, and end up dying of cold and hunger (a metaphor for passing one's life in vain without real attainment).”
[Rely with one bowl upon the ten directions, with one body upon the great earth]

A verse says: “One bowl, the meals of a thousand homes; a lone body, roaming ten thousand miles; to settle the matter of birth and death (to end the great matter of birth and death), begging one's way through the spring and autumn (begging alms to carry on, as spring goes and autumn comes, year after year).”
[Begging alms]

A monk lives by carrying a bowl and begging for food, with no fixed home, no distinction of rich or poor, and no choice; while on pilgrimage he begs alms in proper order, and wherever he arrives is his temporary place of rest.

blocks.text: Suffering Again the Turmoil of War

inline.s: [When the imperial army first took the three Wu regions, bandits from the lakes suddenly rose, and the whole
hé
complete)

city fled in disorder. After a long while the situation settled, and they gradually gathered again. The Bodhisattva said: “Recently, in the upheaval of the thirteenth day of the sixth month, were you not terrified? You should know that all of this comes from kalpas without beginning during which you could not cultivate goodness but widely created evil karma; therefore, life after life, you cannot escape these calamities. As in the time of Emperor Wu of Liang, when eight of you were scattered by the turmoil of war, and today you meet again with the upheaval of war, fleeing with no place left. This shows that if sentient beings cannot transcend the three realms of existence and realize non-arising, then in the end the retributions of causes and conditions will be inescapable to the very last. You are fortunate to have survived, but it was most perilous. The karmic fruits of the three times are alarming and fearful, yet you still do not single-mindedly practice the Way and escape the wheel of suffering early; in another life, this
(a calamity like this)
will be endless. Alas! Alas!]

When the imperial army (the Qing troops) first took the three Wu regions (Suzhou, Changzhou, and Huzhou), bandits from the lakes suddenly rose, and the whole city fled in disorder. After a long while the situation settled, and everyone gradually calmed down and gathered again. The Bodhisattva said: “Recently, in the upheaval of the thirteenth day of the sixth month, were you not terrified? You should know that all of this comes from kalpas without beginning during which you could not cultivate goodness but widely created evil karma; therefore, life after life, you cannot escape these calamities. As in the time of Emperor Wu of Liang, you eight were scattered by the turmoil of war, and today you meet again with the upheaval of war, fleeing with no place left. This shows that if sentient beings cannot transcend the three realms of existence and realize non-arising, then in the end the retributions of causes and conditions will be inescapable to the very last. You are fortunate to have survived, but it was most perilous. The karmic fruits of the three times are alarming and fearful, yet you still do not single-mindedly practice the Way and escape the wheel of suffering early; then in another life, a calamity like this will be endless. Alas! Alas!”

[When the imperial army first took the three Wu regions, bandits from the lakes suddenly rose, and the whole city fled in disorder] The Dharma assembly of the Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing was held in Wu City, beginning on the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month in the guiwei year (
) of the Chongzhen reign of the Ming dynasty, and ending on the second day of the tenth month in the dinghai year (
) of the Shunzhi reign of the Qing dynasty - a little over four years, twenty-four assemblies in all. During this time, in

, the Qing troops conquered Yangzhou, slaughtering the city for ten days and killing eight hundred thousand people; then they took Jiangling, killing one hundred and thirty thousand. Wu City is present-day Suzhou, below Jiangling and bordering Lake Tai. [Three realms of existence]

The birth-and-death of the three realms has causes and fruits, hence they are called the “three realms of existence.” 1. The realm of desire (kāmadhātu): the birth-and-death of the realm of desire; 2. The realm of form (rūpadhātu): the birth-and-death of the realm of form; 3. The realm of formlessness (ārūpyadhātu): the birth-and-death of the realm of formlessness.
[Non-arising]
The true principle of nirvāṇa, which has no arising and no ceasing, is therefore called non-arising.

[The Bodhisattva instructed Shen Yuanhui, saying: “Generally, for those who cultivate the Pure Land, the thing to avoid most is mixing. What is mixing? It is when one both recites sutras and holds mantras, both holds assemblies and likes to speak of aimless Chan, and also talks about fortune and misfortune, and about seeing spirits and ghosts - this is mixing. Since one mixes, the mind is not single-minded; and since the mind is not single-minded, seeing the Buddha and being reborn are hard - is this not wasting one's whole life? You now should do none of these at all, only earnestly hold to the one phrase ‘Amitābha Buddha,’ wishing to be reborn in the Pure Land; after a long time, when the practice matures, you will not take a wrong turn. I will now give you a verse; practice accordingly: A single phrase of Amitābha holds all dharmas; sound and mind rely on each other, thinking on this and again on this. The response is inconceivable: the lotus blooms in the pond of seven treasures.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Shen Yuanhui, saying: “Generally, for those who cultivate the Pure Land, the thing to avoid most is mixing. What is mixing? It is when one both recites sutras and holds mantras, both holds assemblies and likes to speak of aimless Chan, and also talks about fortune and misfortune and about seeing spirits and ghosts - this is mixing. Since one mixes, the mind is not single-minded; and since the mind is not single-minded, seeing the Buddha and being reborn are hard - is this not wasting one's whole life? You now should do none of these at all, only earnestly hold to the one phrase ‘Amitābha Buddha,’ wishing to be reborn in the Pure Land; after a long time, when the practice matures, you will not take a wrong path (you will not go astray). I will now give you a verse; practice accordingly: A single phrase of Amitābha holds all dharmas; sound and mind rely on each other, thinking on this and again on this. The response is inconceivable: the lotus blooms in the pond of seven treasures.”
[The Bodhisattva instructed Dingkai
kǎi
saying: “You have met with a great calamity and were fortunate to escape. From now on you should deeply reflect on your past faults and cut off your later offenses
qiān
transgression)
. Furthermore, do not have an agitated mind or a contentious spirit, do not give free rein to your ambitions or display your abilities, and thereby leave behind
yí jué,
bequeath)

a disaster to your body. Now I set your name as Kai. What does Kai mean? Compassion and benevolence. With compassion establish yourself, with benevolence extend to things. In fame and rank, gain is not a cause for joy, and loss not a cause for sorrow. Only devote yourself to nurturing a good heart and firming good conduct, so as to repay the four kinds of kindness above.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Dingkai, saying: “You have met with a great calamity and were fortunate to escape. From today onward, you should deeply reflect on past faults and cut off future offenses. Furthermore, do not have an agitated mind or a contentious spirit, do not give free rein to your ambitions or display your abilities, and thereby bring disaster upon yourself. Now I give you a name: Kai. What does ‘Kai’ mean? Compassion and benevolence. With compassion establish yourself, with benevolence extend to things. In fame and rank, gain is not enough to rejoice, and loss not enough to grieve. Only wholeheartedly devote yourself to nurturing your good heart and firming good conduct, so as to repay the four kinds of kindness.”

[With compassion establish oneself, with benevolence extend to things] With compassion (kindness) to conduct and cultivate oneself; with benevolence (universal love) to extend kindness to all things. [Four kinds of kindness] The kindness of parents (family), of sentient beings (society), of the land (the nation), and of the Three Jewels (the Buddhist order). [Three Jewels] The Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Sangha-jewel. All Buddhas form the Buddha-jewel; the Dharma spoken by the Buddhas forms the Dharma-jewel; those who practice the Dharma spoken by the Buddhas form the Sangha-jewel.
[At one time, the Bodhisattva descended upon the Dharma assembly. Scholars and commoners,
(Confucian students and ordinary people)

over thirty in number, with unresolved doubts, all came to ask for guidance. The Bodhisattva, pitying these people, who though all possessed a sincere heart yet did not know the correct path of practice, then graciously instructed: “Today's gathering may be said to be one of affinity, but if I were to speak to you of the Buddha Dharma, which you are not accustomed to hearing, I fear it would be hard for you to believe and enter. It would be better to take up a passage from a worldly classic, a Confucian book, and discuss it with you, so that perhaps you may believe one or two phrases. The Doctrine of the Mean says: ‘Some practice it with ease, some practice it for benefit, some practice it by force.’”]

At one time, the Bodhisattva descended upon the Dharma assembly. Scholars and commoners, over thirty in number, had unresolved doubts in their minds and all came to consult and seek guidance. The Bodhisattva, pitying the people present, who though all possessed a sincere heart yet did not know the correct path of practice, then graciously instructed: “Today's gathering may be said to be one of affinity, but if I were to speak to you of the Buddha Dharma, since you have not often heard it in the past, I fear it would be hard for you to believe and enter all at once. It would be better to take up a passage from a Confucian classic and explain it to you, so that perhaps you may believe one or two phrases. The Doctrine of the Mean says: ‘Some practice it with ease, some practice it for benefit, some practice it by force.’”
[The Doctrine of the Mean]

One of the basic classics of Confucianism. Originally a chapter in the Book of Rites, traditionally attributed to Zisi, the grandson of Confucius. In the Southern Song, Zhu Xi grouped it with the Analects, the Mencius, and the Great Learning as the ‘Four Books.’
[Some practice it with ease, some practice it for benefit, some practice it by force] The full text of this passage is: “
Some practice it with ease, some practice it for benefit, some practice it by force; and when they succeed, it is one and the same.

” Because the scholars of the time knew the Four Books by heart, and the common people were also steeped in them, the Bodhisattva here quoted only the first three clauses, quoting the latter part later on. The meaning of this passage is
: some people do it as a matter of course, some do it because there is benefit in it, and some must be forced to do it; yet once the deed is accomplished, the result is one and the same.

[As it appears today, let alone ‘practicing with ease’ and ‘practicing for benefit,’ even one who ‘practices by force’ is not to be found. Just as with you: ever since you met me, you have also resolved to practice goodness by force, yet there are those who give it up all at once, or gradually fall into slackness. What is the reason? It is only that they take the word ‘good’ too lightly. They say that practicing good brings no merit, and is not as effective as doing evil. But they do not realize that if practicing good truly brought no merit, why would the sages and worthies of old, never committing the slightest evil, yet in doing good exert themselves to the utmost, reaching full twelve-tenths of satisfaction?

Now as for ‘practicing with ease’ and ‘practicing for benefit,’ let alone speaking of them, even one who ‘practices by force’ is not to be found. Just as with you: ever since you met me, you have also resolved to practice goodness by force, yet there are those who give it up all at once, or gradually fall into slackness. What is the reason? It is only that they take the word ‘good’ too lightly, so it is hard for it to take effect. They think that practicing good brings no merit, and is not as effective as doing evil. But they do not realize that if practicing good truly brought no merit, why would the sages and worthies of old, never committing the slightest evil, yet in doing good exert themselves to the utmost, reaching full twelve-tenths of satisfaction?

[“If doing evil truly were effective, why then do the benevolent and noble people of old, not only not seek what is effective, but on the contrary do what brings no merit? Moreover, as for those who do evil now, although they gain advantage for the moment, in the end how many have a good ending, a good demise, a good reputation, or good descendants to extend their generations? Again, like a small child of a few years, who upon hearing someone called a good person knows to praise him - is this not the great advantage of doing good? And upon hearing someone called an evil person, becomes angry - is this not the great disadvantage of doing evil?

If doing evil truly were effective, why then do the benevolent and noble people of old, not do the effective thing, but on the contrary do what brings no merit? Moreover, as for those who do evil now, although they gain advantage for the moment, in the end how many have a good ending, a good demise, a good reputation, or good descendants to extend their generations? Again, like a small child of only a few years, who upon hearing that this is a good person knows to praise him - is this not the great advantage of doing good? And upon hearing that this is an evil person, becomes angry - is this not the great disadvantage of doing evil?

[“This matter is very easy to understand. It is not that you are not intelligent and truly do not know. It is only that you are not able to turn to good with a genuine heart, and therefore did not carefully examine for a moment. So in daily life, when you give a coin, you must also tell others about it; when you have a good word, you must also tell others about it. All this is doing things from the outside, without the least realizing where the great sages and worthies apply their minds to their own utmost concerns; and finding it of no flavor, you cast it away.

This matter is very easy to understand. It is not that you are not intelligent and truly do not know. It is only that you are not able to turn to good with a genuine heart, and therefore did not carefully examine for a moment. So in daily life, when you give a coin, you must also tell others about it; when you have a good word, you must also tell others about it. All this is doing things from the outside, without the least realizing where the great sages and worthies apply their minds to their own utmost concerns; and finding it of no flavor, you cast it away.

[“You today, if you truly take a genuine heart and do genuine deeds, without the least delusion or covetousness in between, calm and at ease, content with Heaven and knowing your lot, holding fast to what is within your own control - seeing no lifelong thing to pray for, no ending to ask after, no poverty or wealth of the Five Elements and Eight Characters to divine, no fortune or misfortune, gain or loss to pursue or avoid. Then naturally no calamity is not dispelled, no blessing does not arrive, the Way increases with time, virtue accumulates with the years, and to become a sage or a worthy is not difficult. This is the certain real outcome for you in the future; therefore it is said, ‘and when they succeed, it is one and the same.’ If on the contrary, then in life one is a petty man without restraint, and in death a rotting weed - how lamentable!”]

You today, if you truly take a genuine heart and do genuine deeds, without the least delusion or covetousness in between, calm and at ease, content with Heaven and knowing your lot, holding fast to what is within your own control - seeing no lifelong thing to pray for, no ending to ask after, no poverty or wealth of the Five Elements and Eight Characters to divine, no fortune or misfortune, gain or loss to pursue or avoid. Then naturally no calamity is not dispelled, no blessing does not arrive, the Way increases with time, virtue accumulates with the years, and to become a sage or a worthy is not difficult. This is the certain real outcome for you in the future; therefore it is said, ‘and when they succeed, it is one and the same.’ If on the contrary, then in life one is an unbridled petty man, and in death a rotting, stinking weed - how lamentable!”
[Woven into one's own concerns] Intimately related to oneself. [Coveting
jìyú
Hope to obtain (something one should not obtain).
[When the Bodhisattva had spoken these words, he fell silent and remained. At that time, the people still
yóngyóng
a look of eager expectation)

in attendance, and there were even those who bowed again and offered prayers. The Bodhisattva said: “How great is your folly! Hearing such words, you do not even give rise to a mind of longing or a thought of turning back, but merely want to ask about the matters of children and family in your breasts, and only then are satisfied. Sorrowful indeed! Sorrowful indeed! Yet the Bodhisattva's great compassion is inexhaustible, so I will say some more old words to awaken you from your deluded dream.”]

When the Bodhisattva had spoken these words, he fell silent and remained. At that time, the people were still expecting and hoping, and there were even those who bowed again and offered prayers. The Bodhisattva said: “You people are truly too foolish. Hearing these words of mine, you do not even give rise to a mind of longing or a thought of turning back (examining and correcting oneself), but merely want to ask about the matters of children and family in your breasts, and only then are satisfied. Sorrowful indeed! Sorrowful indeed! Yet the Bodhisattva's great compassion is boundless, so I will say some more old words (words handed down from antiquity) to awaken you from your deluded dream.”
[“First, those who study the Way: when their emotions are not upright, their nature is then estranged; when the mind is not firm, virtue is then lacking
(the same as ‘lacking’)
. Often they are careful for a moment
(an instant)

and change in a blink. Such people may be called the sort for whom there is no ground to fashion them; it is hard for them to enter the Way. It is not that the sage is weary of teaching people and deliberately cuts them off. Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!]

First, those who study the Way: when their emotions are not upright, their nature is then estranged; when the mind is not firm, virtue is then lacking (the same as ‘lacking’). Often they are careful for an instant and change in a blink. Such people are the sort for whom there is no ground to fashion them; it is hard for them to enter the Way. This is not because the sage is weary of teaching people and deliberately does not instruct them. Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!

[When the emotions are not upright, the nature is estranged] When the emotions have greed, hatred, and delusion, they are not upright. If so, then the original nature leaves its station and becomes deluded. [When the mind is not firm, virtue is lacking] When the resolve of the mind is not firm, then virtue and morality are lacking.

[“First, in the world there are also many intelligent and upward-striving scholars, yet they are obstructed by their own self-righteous opinions and fail to become great vessels. For once a person is self-righteous, he will certainly not be willing to humbly seek correction from one who has the Way. Those he associates with on ordinary days will certainly be a class of mediocre and lowly fellows, who praise one another. In whatever they do, they cannot hear their own faults face to face, and so their virtue and career are in peril. Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!

First, in the world there are also many intelligent and upward-striving scholars, yet they are obstructed by their own self-righteous opinions and fail to become great vessels. For once a person is self-righteous, he will certainly not be willing to humbly seek correction from one who has the Way. Those they associate with on ordinary days will certainly be the most mediocre and lowly of fellows, who praise one another. In whatever they do, they cannot hear their own faults face to face, and so their virtue and career are very much in peril. Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!

[“First, worldly people crave gain and are intent on forcing things. They do not understand that even gaining a single coin depends on destiny, much less the greater things like fame, rank, wealth, and honor! They say: ‘I can seek it with intelligence and strength.’ If so, then the azure heavens above and the majestic spirits - would they be of no use? Even if one obtains it by force, it is because it was destined to be had, not because Heaven took pity and gave it to you for having used so much sordid scheming. Thus, those who seek by force: they have disgrace but not glory, loss but not gain, the calamity of
lù
the same as ‘executed’)
bodily harm, but no merit in benefiting living beings
(sentient beings)
; they have the disaster of harming virtue but no fortune of advancing in good. Heaven loathes them and the spirits cast them off. Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!]

First, worldly people crave gain and are all intent on forcing things. They do not understand that even gaining a single coin depends on destiny, much less the greater things like fame, rank, wealth, and honor! Some say: ‘I can seek it by using intelligence and strength.’ If so, then the azure heavens above and the majestic spirits - would they be of no use? Even if one obtains it by force, it is because it was destined to have it, not because Heaven took pity and gave it to you for having used so much sordid scheming. Thus, those who seek by force: they have disgrace but not glory, loss but not gain, the calamity of losing life, but no merit in benefiting living beings (in benefiting sentient beings); they have the disaster of harming virtue but no fortune of advancing in good. Heaven loathes them and the spirits cast them off. Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!

[“First, the greatest kindness in the world is none other than that of parents. While parents are alive, they are a living Buddha before the hall; after they have passed, one may still seek to repay them. Consider: where does this body come from? By what is it grown? Yet one cannot return to the root and trace the source, exert utmost heart and strength to serve them respectfully and obey them compliantly, but instead bears resentment toward parents and disregards them, benefits only one's own wife and children and fails to support them, and even worse, knows not when they are ill, and does not bury them when they die, or even retaliates for a single word as if they were a stranger - such people are not even as good as beasts. Alas! Is it possible that a person is worse than beasts? How fearful! Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!”]

First, the greatest kindness in the world is none other than that of parents. While parents are alive, they are a living Buddha before the hall; after they have passed, one may still seek to repay them. Think it over: where does this body come from? By what is it grown? Yet one cannot return to the root and trace the source, exert utmost heart and strength toward parents, serving them respectfully and obeying them compliantly, but instead bears resentment toward parents and disregards them, caring only for wife and children and failing to support parents filially, and even worse, knows not when parents are ill, and does not bury them when they die, or retaliates even for a single word, treating them as strangers - these are all worse than beasts. Alas! Is it possible that being human, one is not even as good as a beast? How fearful! Whoever among you has discernment, consider this!”

blocks.text: The Desire to Be an Official

inline.s: [Someone
(a certain person)

wanted to become an official and asked whether he could obtain it. The Bodhisattva said: “As for being an official, you should not even think of it! You must know: to have mastered the classics and histories is called literary; to be versed in the art of war
(the ancient military books, the Six Secret Teachings and the Three Strategies, and also military manuals in general)
is called martial; to exceed others in bodily strength
lǚ lì,
physical strength)

is called courage; and to stand out in intelligence is called talent. Consider for yourself: do you have any one of these? If you have not even one of the four, then to become an official is nothing but courting luck. And to court luck, your thought is already not upright. Once you become an official, you then put on the air of authority and rely on power, only tormenting the weary people to fill your own belly, never thinking to do some good for the nation and the people. So the evil you accumulate deepens daily, and unaware of repentance, in the next life you will surely be reborn among such animals as oxen, horses, camels, and mules that use their strength to repay men. Like the sort of animals in the present wars and battle-lines: all are descendants of those who in former lives usurped emoluments and coveted merit, with not the slightest merit toward the world.”]

Someone wanted to become an official and asked the Bodhisattva whether he could obtain it. The Bodhisattva said: “As for being an official, you should not even think of it! You must know: to have mastered the classics and histories is called literary; to be versed in the art of war is called martial; to exceed others in bodily strength is called courage; and to stand out in intelligence is called talent. Consider for yourself: do you have any one of these abilities? If you have not even one of the four, then to become an official is nothing but courting luck. And to court luck, your thought is already not upright. Once you become an official, you then put on the air of authority and rely on power, only tormenting the weary people to fill your own belly, never considering doing some good for the nation and the people. So the evil you accumulate deepens daily, and unaware of repentance, in the next life you will surely be reborn among such animals as oxen, horses, camels, and mules that have strength, serving labors to repay debts. Like the sort of animals in the present wars and battle-lines: all are those who in former lives usurped emoluments and coveted merit, with not the slightest merit toward the world.”
[“Moreover, concerning the principle of retribution, its distance or nearness has no fixed time; it either brings calamity in the present life or affects descendants. For example, the sort
(a kind)
of criminals now in prison
líng yǔ
, also written ‘líng yǔ,’ a prison)

, who suffer execution, whose offspring are unworthy, or who are cut off without descendants - such are these. Again, harming good people and taking their wealth and goods is called things of inhumanity and injustice. Offer them to ancestors, and the ancestors' offenses increase
qiān
, transgression)

; serve the gods with them, and the gods grow angry; present them to the Buddhas, sages, and worthies, and they will surely shed tears for it; present them to a benevolent and virtuous person, and he will on the contrary feel shame. Even if their evil is not at its extreme, yet grievances stand in mutual requital, and in the later life they will surely be reborn as a kind of sheep, pig, chicken, or dog - animals lacking strength to repay men - and as the sort of most poor, lowly, and bitterly suffering people in the world. Again, this class that courts luck: even if in office they do some good, it is unavoidable that there is selfishness within the public, and evil within the good. The retribution of sin and blessing is spread about without letting a single hair slip: to covet a finite and glorious name and receive the evil fruits of many lives. To court luck in becoming an official, drowning the mind in profit and desire, the evil consequences as discussed above inevitably follow - how could it not be fearful!”]

Moreover, concerning the principle of retribution, whether it is far or near has no fixed time; it either brings about calamity in the present life or affects descendants. For example, the criminals now in prison, who suffer execution, whose offspring are unworthy, or who are cut off without descendants - such are these. Again, harming good people and taking their wealth and goods is called things of inhumanity and injustice. Use them to sacrifice to ancestors, and the ancestors' offenses increase; use them to serve the gods, and the gods grow angry; use them to present to the Buddhas, sages, and worthies, and they will surely shed tears for it; use them to honor a benevolent and virtuous person, and he will on the contrary feel shame. Even if their evil is not at its extreme, yet grievances stand in mutual requital, and in the later life they will surely be reborn as a kind of sheep, pig, chicken, or dog - animals lacking strength to do labor - repaying their debts with their own flesh and blood, and as the sort of most poor, lowly, and bitterly suffering people in the world. Again, this class that courts luck: even if in office they do some good, it is unavoidable that there is selfishness within the public, and evil within the good. The retribution of sin and blessing is spread about without letting a single hair slip: to covet a finite and glorious name and receive the evil fruits of many lives. To court luck in becoming an official, drowning the mind in profit and desire, the evil consequences as discussed above inevitably follow - how could one not fear!”
[Wang Dingyou sought a child. The Bodhisattva said: “From now on, do not kill living beings, do not eat strange food
(meaning rare delicacies)
, do not be over-indulgent or give way to anger. Why? Killing harms the mercy of heaven and earth and goes against the way of nurturing
zhǎng
. Eating strange food surely increases lust and defilement, or may bring on a terrible disease. Giving way to anger then wounds
qiāng
kill, harm)
and diminishes the span of life, violently breaking the primal harmony
(the fundamental harmony)

, and also much offends against the taboos of yin and yang. You should forever observe these three, single-mindedly support your old mother, extend benefits and practice compassion, relieve the poor and rescue the suffering, widely practice hidden virtue, and accumulate without ceasing; Heaven will surely bestow
(confer)
on you good offspring
yìn
children, descendants)

Wang Dingyou sought a child. The Bodhisattva said: “From now on, do not kill living beings, do not eat rare delicacies, do not be over-indulgent or give way to anger. Why? Killing harms the mercy of heaven and earth and departs from the way of nurturing (
zhǎng

). Eating rare delicacies surely increases lust and defilement, or may bring on a terrible disease. Giving way to anger then destroys the span of life, violently breaking the primordial harmony (the fundamental harmony), and also much offends against the taboos of yin and yang. You should forever observe these three, single-mindedly support your old mother, extend benefits and practice compassion, relieve the poor and rescue the suffering, widely practice hidden virtue, and accumulate without ceasing; Heaven will surely bestow good children and grandchildren on you.”
[Extending benefits] Giving the good to others. [Practicing compassion] Causing sentient beings to be at peace and happy.

blocks.text: Do Not Be Intimate with Unruly Youths

inline.s: [The Bodhisattva bestowed a verse on Lu Dingxi, saying: “Be close to the mature and seasoned; do not be intimate with unruly youths. The gentleman advances upward; you
(you all)
should follow. To urge your mother to practice is great filial piety; be sincere and reverent, and observe the Bodhisattva's teaching.”]
The Bodhisattva instructed Lu Dingxi with a verse: “Be close to the mature and seasoned; do not be intimately familiar with (
xiá

intimate) unruly youths. The gentleman advances upward; you all should follow (you should emulate). To urge your mother to practice is great filial piety; be sincere and reverent, and observe the Bodhisattva's teaching.”
[Unruly youths]
Young people of bad conduct who act lawlessly.
[Advance upward]
One who cultivates virtue and penetrates through to benevolence and righteousness.

[Again he instructed, saying: “When you return, earnestly urge your mother to recite the Buddha with utmost sincerity and seek rebirth in the Pure Land. If she cannot be vegetarian, do not force her, but she must not kill living beings. If she is willing to turn toward Amitābha, she will of her own accord give up flesh and blood. This is the foremost filial conduct in the world; you should strive for it.”]

The Bodhisattva again instructed, saying: “When you return, repeatedly and earnestly urge your mother to recite the Buddha with utmost sincerity and seek rebirth in the land of Ultimate Bliss. If she cannot be vegetarian, do not force her, but she must not kill living beings. If she is willing to turn toward Amitābha Buddha, she will of her own accord give up eating flesh and blood. This is the foremost filial conduct in the world; you should diligently do it.”

blocks.text: Teaching Given to Each in Turn

inline.s: [At that time, the Bodhisattva's work of guiding beings was at an end, and so he summoned all his disciples together and gave instruction to each.]
At that time, the Bodhisattva's work of guiding beings was at an end, and so he gathered all his disciples together and instructed them one by one.

[He instructed Dingmian, saying: “Your name is Dingmian; you should take the style name Zikai (self-opening). Strive in your practice and you will of yourself attain the awakening of supreme bodhi, become a good friend, and continue the Buddha's wisdom-life. Do not
(you must not)
give up on yourself.”]

The Bodhisattva instructed Dingmian, saying: “Your name is ‘Dingmian’; you should take the style name ‘Zikai’ (self-opening). Be sure to strive in your practice, and you will of yourself attain the awakening of supreme bodhi, become a good friend, and continue the Buddha's wisdom-life. Do not give up on yourself.”
[Haō (a stylistic name)]
It refers to an additional appellation a person takes apart from his given name and courtesy name. For example: “Li Bai, courtesy name Taibai, style name the Hermit of the Green Lotus.”

[Dingkai asked about the purport of the three contemplations in a single mind. The Bodhisattva said: “The three contemplations of the Tiantai school have their wonder in the center of the mind. If one knows the center of the mind, the way is entirely realized.” He had [Dingkai] stand with Dingmian
(Zikai)
side by side
(he had him stand shoulder to shoulder with Dingmian)
, and gave a gatha: “One opening and a second opening, today you come again; the bodhi has its seed, and a wondrous hand plants both.”]

Dingkai asked about the purport of the three contemplations in a single mind, and the Bodhisattva said: “The three contemplations of the Tiantai school have their wonder in the center of the mind. If one knows the center of the mind, the three contemplations in a single mind will be completely understood.” Then the Bodhisattva had him stand side by side with Dingmian (Zikai) and gave a gatha: “Dingkai and Zikai, today you come again; the bodhi naturally has its seed, and a wondrous hand nurtures both.”

[The three contemplations in a single mind (yixin sanguan)] The contemplation method of the Tiantai school. The Tiantai school says that the entire universe of existences all possess the three truths of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, and that these three truths are mutually present and mutually fused: emptiness is provision and middle, provision is emptiness and middle, and the middle is emptiness and provision. If we contemplate in this way within a single mind, it is called “the three contemplations in a single mind.” [The three truths (sandi)] The truth of emptiness, the truth of provisionality, and the truth of the middle. The truth of emptiness means that things are empty of self-substance; the truth of provisionality means that there are merely provisional, condition-arisen appearances; the truth of the middle means that all dharmas are neither empty nor provisional yet both empty and provisional — the real principle of the Middle Way. These three truths were established by the Tiantai school.

[Instructing Shande, he said: “Your head is already shaved; you should know contentment. Think on impermanence and cut off love and desire. Namo Amitābha — thought after thought, constantly in succession.”]

He instructed Shande: “Your head is already shaved (aged and weakened in strength); you should know contentment. Think on impermanence and cut off love and desire. Namo Amitābha — thought after thought, constantly in succession.”

[Instructing Erzhi, he said: “Diligence keeps one from illness; without diligence, illness comes. Do not say that past karma will be repaid only very far off. The compassionate father Amitābha — visit him again and again; this can prolong your years, and how much more dispel illness.”]

He instructed Erzhi: “Diligence keeps one from illness; without diligence, illness comes. Do not say that past karma's recompense is very far off. The compassionate father Amitābha — visit him again and again (constantly); this can bring long life and can also remove sickness and pain.”

[Instructing Chen Daxin, he said: “Growing old without letting go, at death you will surely be entangled. When the debt to children and family is repaid, then you may be happy. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far; do not cut yourself off from it.”]

He instructed Chen Daxin: “Growing old without letting go (at an age still not shedding one's entanglements), at death you will surely be entangled (at death you will certainly be burdened by them). When the debt to children and family is repaid, then you may be happy. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far; do not cut yourself off from it.”

[Instructing Shen Yuanhui, he said: “Dwelling deep and hidden without showing oneself — this is called upholding the precepts. If one floats to the surface and out, before long one will surely fail. Since the thought is not true, one cannot be free; fortune and misfortune, good and ill — you yourself make them strange.”]

He instructed Shen Yuanhui: “Dwelling deep and hidden without showing oneself — this is called upholding the precepts. If one floats to the surface and out, before long one will surely fail. Since the thought is not true, one cannot be free; fortune and misfortune, good and ill — you yourself make them strange (fortune and misfortune have no door; only people call them upon themselves).”

[Instructing Du Yijian, he said: “The good is righteousness; the not-good is not righteousness. Righteousness and good are not two; what is seen is only righteousness. Taking righteousness as one's view, one does not see the not-righteous. When one sees the not-righteous, then seeing has nothing to see that is righteous.”]

He instructed Du Yijian: “The good is righteousness; the not-good is then not righteousness. Righteousness and good are not two; what is seen is only righteousness. Taking righteousness as one's view, one does not see the not-righteous; taking the not-righteous as one's view, one does not see righteousness.”
[Righteousness (yi)]
The principle or action that is just and fitting.
[Instructing the female disciple Yian, he said: “Is it because of illness that you do not recite the Buddha? Ah
yī
, an exclamation)
! The more severe the illness, the more diligent the recitation should be. If one lets the illness reach the point where one cannot recite, then one has erred indeed.”]

He instructed the female disciple Yian: “Is it because you are ill that you do not recite the Buddha? Ah! The more serious the illness, the more diligent the recitation should be. If you let the illness reach the point where you cannot recite, then you have erred indeed.”
[Instructing Wuxiu, he said: “Is a foot-long jade disk a treasure? The inch of time should be treasured. Think rightly on Amitābha — the light of faith is brilliant
(resplendent and shining)
. Do not cling to former acquaintances, or the road ahead will be forever lost.”]

He instructed Wuxiu: “A foot-long jade disk is not really precious; the inch of time is precious and should be cherished. Think rightly on Amitābha, and the light of faith shines brilliantly. Do not cling to the friends of old acquaintance, lest the practice of the Way be lost forever.”
[A foot-long jade disk (chibi)] A jade disk one foot in diameter. [An inch of time (cunyin)] A brief span of time. The Huainanzi
in the chapter “Tracing the Way” says: “The sage does not prize a foot of jade, but values an inch of time, because time is hard to get and easy to lose.”
[Instructing Changshe, he said: “Having a mouth, yet as if dumb; having ears, yet as if deaf. Break with the crowd and leave the world, and the Way is then exalted.”]

He instructed Changshe: “Having a mouth, yet as if dumb; having ears, yet as if deaf. Break with the crowd and leave the world, and the Way is then exalted (only when the practice of the Way is accomplished can it be grand).”
[Instructing Changyuan, he said: “Let your conduct not be negligent; negligence is not that of a bhikṣu. Those who ruin themselves have many sorrows after death.”]
He instructed Changyuan: “Your cultivation must not be negligent; negligence is not that of a bhikṣu. Those who ruin their own practice of the Way will have great troubles afterward.”
[Instructing Dingmao, he said: “You are one of the Way; you should purify your mind. Those who can purify the mind can transcend the multitude.”]
He instructed Dingmao: “You are one of the Way (you are a cultivator of the Way); you should purify your mind. Those who can purify the mind can transcend the multitude.”

[Instructing Dingsui, he said: “Honesty is a treasure, yet it also has its shortcoming: if one is only this, it merely suffices for food and warmth. What is the use of leaving home? Wish to be free of delusion and affliction; you should give rise to the mind of the Way, and not let the time pass in vain.”]

He instructed Dingsui: “Honesty is a treasure, yet it also has its shortcoming: if one is merely this, it only suffices for food and warmth. What is the use of leaving home? Wish to be free of afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion; you should give rise to the mind of the Way, and not let the time pass in vain.”
[Instructing Zha Dinghong, he said: “The Bodhisattva's gatha is like the everyday tea and rice. Go back and tell your mother: the matter of her own [rebirth] should be attended to early.”]

He instructed Zha Dinghong: “The Bodhisattva's gatha is like everyday tea and rice. Go back and tell your mother: the great matter of being reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss must be attended to early.”
[Go back and tell your mother: attend to your own matter early]
The Bodhisattva's instruction to Zha Dinghong's mother is found in the section “Wrong Views Lead the Way Astray.”
[Instructing Chen Dingzhuan, he said: “Only Heaven is highest, and it sees everything. Guard your first mind — take care that it changes not even a little.”]
He instructed Chen Dingzhuan: “Only Heaven is highest and sees everything. You must protect your first mind and be very careful not to let it retreat.”
[Instructing Daben, he said: “To reach the root is to be without root; all conditions should be stilled. Why do you not dwell in peace, and are still bustling
jíjí
? One day you will let go; then the man farms and the woman weaves. Reflecting on your former life, you will weep alone.”]

He instructed Daben: “To reach the root is to be without root (the world is an illusion); all conditions should be stilled (all conditions are impermanent). Why do you not cultivate with a still mind, but still eagerly pursue outward with all your might? Once life ends, the next life is again the wheel of rebirth; reflecting on your former life of no effort, you have only regret and tears.”

[One day you will let go; then the man farms and the woman weaves] Once life ends, the next life is again the man farming and the woman weaving (a metaphor that if in this life one has not realized the Way, in the next life one is still within the wheel of rebirth).

[Then, when the Bodhisattva had instructed each one, he said again to them: “Since I have descended here, all my words are the essential wonders of practice. If you can contemplate them at all times and earnestly follow them, you will surely be born in the highest grade. The Bodhisattva will from now on come no more. You disciples should each exert yourselves, and do not make this assembly vain.”]

Then, when the Bodhisattva had instructed each one, he said again to the assembly: “Since I have descended to this place, all my words are the essential wonders of practice. If you can contemplate them at all times and earnestly follow them, you will certainly be reborn in the highest grade. The Bodhisattva will from now on come no more. You disciples should each exert yourselves, and not have attended this assembly in vain.”

[Then, hearing the Bodhisattva's words, the disciples all wept in sorrowful attachment and could not raise their eyes. The Bodhisattva said to them: “Disciples, you think that because the Bodhisattva will not descend again, you might grow negligent and from then on lose your footing. But in truth it is not so. Why? From now on, your vigor is only your own vigor; leaving the dusty path
(the same as the world of dust)

and ascending to the realm of sages — this is the doing of the greatly wise and the greatly worthy. If you are negligent, that too is your own negligence; turning your back on the great Way and entering the mud — this is the doing of the ignorant and the foolish. Disciples, you have only to go forward and not give rise to attachment; only press on with effort, and there is no need for sorrow.”]

Then, hearing the Bodhisattva say this, the disciples all wept in sorrowful attachment and could not raise their eyes. The Bodhisattva said to them: “Disciples, because the Bodhisattva will not descend again, you fear that you might grow negligent and from then on lose your footing. But in truth it is not so. Why? From now on, your vigor is your own vigor (vigor depends on yourself); leaving the Saha world and ascending to Ultimate Bliss — this is the doing of the greatly wise and the greatly worthy. If you are negligent, that too is your own negligence (negligence also depends on yourself); turning your back on the great Way and entering the mud — this is the doing of the ignorant and the foolish. Disciples, you have only to press forward and not give rise to attachment; only press on with urgent effort, and there is no need for sorrow.”

[After a while, he again admonished: “You must not again entertain the thought that the Bodhisattva will descend. Why? The establishment of the phoenix planchette is originally that on which spirits and ghosts rely; it is not the constant work of the great Bodhisattva's manifestation. If you follow the teaching without fail, and give rise toward the Bodhisattva a mind of reverence and the thought of [an encounter] hard to obtain
(the thought of something extremely hard to encounter)
, that is the great place of repaying kindness.”]

After a while, the Bodhisattva again instructed: “You must not again entertain the thought that the Bodhisattva will descend. Why? The planchette is originally what spirits and ghosts rely upon; this is not the constant work of the great Bodhisattva's manifestation. If you follow the teaching without fail, and give rise toward the Bodhisattva a mind of reverence and the thought of something extremely hard to encounter, that is the great place of repaying kindness.”

[At that time, although the disciples heard the Dharma admonition, they still gathered around, unwilling to disperse. The Bodhisattva again admonished: “Disciples, in his past causal practice the Bodhisattva had a great connection with you. Although he will not descend again from now on, you must not entertain the thought of [his being] far away. You should know that the Enlightened, Bright, Wondrous Practice [Bodhisattva] is at all times before your eyes, following you without leaving. Take care that you do not for a single day become lax, and thereby abandon the Enlightened Bright Wondrous Practice yourselves.”]

At that time, although the disciples heard the Bodhisattva's Dharma admonition, they still gathered around, unwilling to disperse. The Bodhisattva again instructed: “Disciples, in his past causal practice the Bodhisattva had a great connection with you. Although he will not descend again from now on, you must not entertain the thought of the Bodhisattva's being far away. You should know that the Enlightened, Bright, Wondrous Practice [Bodhisattva] is at all times before your eyes, following you without leaving. Take care that you do not for a single day become indolent, or else you yourselves abandon the Enlightened Bright Wondrous Practice!”

[After a little while, he again admonished: “Disciples, since the Dharma assembly is finished, you should each disperse. The Bodhisattva comes without origin and goes without destination. Do not only sit staring and guarding; the Bodhisattva is surely not on a sheet of paper. Let each of you recite one ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha,’ make salutation with utmost sincerity, and receive
(reverently receive)
and put it into practice — that is enough.”]

After a little while, the Bodhisattva again instructed: “Disciples, since the Dharma assembly is already ended, everyone should disperse. The Bodhisattva comes without origin and goes without destination. Do not only sit staring and guarding; the Bodhisattva is after all not on this sheet of paper of the planchette (this means: one should guard the Enlightened Bright Wondrous Practice Bodhisattva in the mind, not guard the Enlightened Bright Wondrous Practice Bodhisattva on the planchette paper). Let each of you recite one ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha,’ make salutation with utmost sincerity, reverently receive my instruction, and earnestly put it into practice — that is enough.”
Reliable Pointers to the Western Land (End)
